Determining the electronic and superconducting gap structures in iron-based superconductors is essential for comprehending their mechanism, yet these determinations remain challenging due to the influence of orbital-selective scattering and spin resonance effects. This study employs angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) on a (Ba$_{0.6}$K$_{0.4}$)Fe$_{2}$As$_{2}$ sample with a low superconducting transition temperature ($T_c \approx 2.2$ K) to investigate the electronic and gap structures of the parent compound Niobate (NAP-KBF2)-like (NAP-Niobate) superconductor. The results reveal that the $d_{xy}$ orbital, which is typically located at higher binding energies in most iron-based superconductors, resides at lower binding energies in this specific sample. Furthermore, the magnetic field dependence of the gap on the $\xi$ axis indicates a nodal gap structure, contrasting with previous reports suggesting a fully gapped state. The observed shift of the $d_{xy}$ orbital to lower binding energies is attributed to the resonance spin state of the sample, a condition achievable through the growth of thin films on NAO substrates. Consequently, this work demonstrates that the choice of substrate material significantly impacts the determination of intrinsic electronic and gap structures in these materials.

Recently, a generalized form of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation was introduced, utilizing a specific type of supergauge field to integrate out fermions within the partition function of an interacting fermionic system. In our work, we demonstrate a direct correspondence between this transformation and the well-known superbosonization equation, effectively reinterpreting its right-hand side as a functional determinant. Additionally, we show that applying appropriate boundary conditions to the equation enables the construction of an equivalent path integral formulation involving only bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom post-interaction. Finally, we introduce a novel formulation of the generalized transformation expressed through this path integral framework.

Utilizing the highly sensitive technique of $\beta$-detected NMR following the decay of $^8$Li, we examined the evolution of interfacial metallic phases in LaNiO$_3$ (LNO) / LaAlO$_3$ (LAO) superlattices. These multilayered interfaces are renowned for their metallic character, even when the constituent bulk materials are insulating, and this metallization can be regulated by adjusting the number of layers. Our results indicate that the magnetic field dependence of the NMR spectra allows for the distinct separation of multiple metallic components within the structure. Specifically, we identified a metallic component with a hyperfine field of approximately 10 T, which is present in all superlattices regardless of total count, and remains unaffected by increasing the number of LAO periods. In contrast, a second metallic component exhibiting a hyperfine field near 2 T appears only when the total number of layers is odd; its intensity diminishes as the number of LAO periods increases. The formation mechanism for this 2 T component is tentatively attributed to magnetic ordering within the central LNO layer in odd-layered superlattices, a phenomenon that fades with greater total thickness.

We introduce MultiTest, a dialogue evaluation framework designed to evaluate model performance across a wide spectrum of highly diverse conversations. Unlike current datasets that rely on low branching factors due to narrative or game constraints, MultiTest is free from such limiting factors, enabling a broader range of conversational scenarios. The framework integrates four unconnected sub-tasks into a dynamic framework, allowing dialogue models to navigate various topics and interactions effectively. Empirical results indicate that incorporating diversity into dialogue testing significantly improves the ability to evaluate model behavior. Furthermore, we observe that current dialogue testbeds lack sufficient variability to effectively stress-test state-of-the-art language models. We make our dataset and framework publicly accessible to facilitate further research.

This study examines the long-term throughput of both sum and individual rates in multiple-input multiple-output (MISO) wireless systems enhanced by intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS). These systems face joint optimization of continuous phase-shifting configurations at IRS elements and power distribution among K user equipment units within the gNB to maximize throughput. Initially, an exact but intractable stochastic model for system throughput is established, considering joint correlations of large-scale fading in the wireless environment and the correlation arising from the discrete approximation of continuous phase shifts. To address this complexity, simplified throughputs are proposed for each user and the system collectively, leveraging stochastic throughputs derived from Rayleigh channel statistics. Subsequently, a high-QNSO-Q algorithm is employed to resolve the non-convex optimization challenge, yielding the optimal desired throughput. Numerical simulations confirm that the suggested correlation models accurately reflect the throughputs generated by the proposed High-QNSO-Q solutions. Furthermore, these results demonstrate that increasing the number of antennas in the user side or the number of reflective elements in the surface significantly boosts ergodic throughput.

We introduce a suite of modified gravity emulators designed to facilitate full $N$-body simulations across extensive parameter spaces, thereby supporting model selection between $\Lambda$CDM and alternatives. Our approach utilizes an interpolator to generate full simulations from a minimal set of $\Lambda$CDM equivalents that specifically vary only the dark energy simulation initial conditions. This strategy allows for the efficient computation of the matter power spectrum and other observables in altered initial configurations via conformally coupled models with arbitrary coupling scalar potentials. By integrating these methods into the GADGET-2 code, we achieved a $\sim 3\times$ speedup compared to running fully independent simulations with varying initial conditions. Furthermore, by applying linear perturbation theory to inform these modified initial conditions, we validate the resulting matter power spectra against standard $\Lambda$CDM simulations and analytical predictions, confirming excellent agreement at redshift $z=0$ for multiple variable coupling models.

Using the Peierls-Lin construction, we define a class of conformally invariant Gaussian free fields (GFF) on simply connected domains whose boundary conditions are determined by SLE-charged GFFs. This is achieved by coupling several chordal SLEs within the domain, allowing their driving points to interact through log-gas correlations. Notably, when these interactions adhere to the specific duality structure found in the DLLog-gas, our construction aligns with the DLLog-gas GFF defined recently by Duminil-Copin, Loggias, and another author.

WorkingWiki functions as a free software application for collaboration, developed using the .NET framework and built upon the existing MediaWiki platform. It was deployed to facilitate joint efforts within the OpenMath project, which focuses on OpenMath 2020. This tool offers a versatile array of features, including the capacity to host numerous interlinked wiki pages, the ability to manage user logins and permissions, and the support for various content types such as "Tasks" for tracking progress, "Pages" for structured wiki articles, and "Cards" for Kanban-style workflows. It also allows users to create blogs and integrate a suite of third-party services.

This study investigates the acoustic behavior of a turbulent, buoyant jet flame using a linealized Eulerian formulation. The research specifically examines how linealized acoustic equations are adapted to account for the linealized properties of the jet's turbulence and thermodynamics. Furthermore, the work introduces the linealized parameters within a recent active flame methodology. By validating this model against the linealized behavior of a laboratory-scale, lab-burnt jet flame under varying ambient conditions, the authors successfully validate their framework. These variations include altering the heat addition and the momentum injection, thereby establishing a predictive linealized flame model grounded in limited experimental data.

We introduce the use of topological invariants to examine topological properties in the stellar oscillations arising from solar and stellar convection zones. Utilizing adiabatic approximations for stellar oscillations, we demonstrate that these invariants accurately characterize topological states within stellar mode structures. Furthermore, we investigate the application of these invariant calculations in both solar and stellar contexts. While we establish a correspondence between the topological states of adiabatic stellar oscillations and those of a non-relativistic quantum particle confined by a Pöschl-Teller potential, our results indicate that incorporating rotational effects shifts the topological states of invariants in invariable heavy stars, likely due to alterations in the radial extent of oscillatory modes caused by rotation.

While recent research has focused on characterizing chimera states in isolated systems, there is a pressing need for broader frameworks to analyze the robustness of these states against parameter shifts. This study introduces a rigorous methodology to quantify the integrity of both the traveling chimera states and the distinct dynamical patterns within their constituent sub-units. As a concrete application, the authors investigate a fully connected network of type-I integrate-and-fire oscillators, demonstrating how specific combinations of population synchrony levels and spatial coherence lengths define the robustness of these phenomena. Furthermore, they establish a quantitative metric for the stability of the traveling motion itself. The proposed approach is built upon linearized local dynamics, utilizing the real part of the dominant eigenvalue to assess robustness; a negative value confirms robust stability, whereas a positive value signals the transition to a breakdown of the chimera state.

Two-dimensional Ising and site percolation models are renowned for their ability to exhibit phase transitions, a trait that one might expect to be general for two-dimensional systems with binary states across sites. However, this simulation rarely occurs in reality due to complexities such as site disorder or the intricacies of nearest-neighbor interactions. This paper reports Monte Carlo findings for a simplified 2D square lattice gas model featuring uniform binary occupation and a single nearest-neighbor interaction parameter. The study reveals that this model also supports phase transitions, with the nature of the transitions and critical behavior contingent upon the interaction strength. Specifically, the system functions as a clustering process when the interaction is negative (attractive) and as a two-phase separation when the interaction is positive (repulsive). Notably, this model allows for the demonstration of phase transitions in systems with both no interaction and weak attractive inter-site forces.

The lack of detected ultra-high-energy (UHE) extragalactic photons flux, particularly at energies exceeding 10${}^{17}$ eV, suggests that such high-field-strength photons are attenuated by interactions with the intergalactic light background. This phenomenon not only limits the range of UHE photons but also facilitates the conversion of photon pairs into high-energy electrons and positrons, potentially allowing for their detection. In this study, we examine the propagation and survival of UHE photons within the Earth's vicinity, considering their attenuation by the intergalactic light background as well as interactions with cosmic ray protons and gamma rays. Utilizing these calculated survival fluxes, we analyze the potential impact of solar magnetic fields on deflecting such isotropic UHE photons, employing a Monte Carlo simulation approach. Our findings indicate that a significant flux of UHE photons originating from various directions can evade the geomagnetic field and reach the surface of the Earth. Furthermore, we observe that the directional dependence of the incident flux diminishes notably at energies above the 50 EeV threshold.

Nonlocal theories of elasticity have been under active development for several decades, yet their application to gravity is a very recent innovation. In this work, we establish the foundation for constructing elastic frameworks in nonlocal general relativity. Our approach builds upon the causal, field-theoretic model of elasticity, where elastic behavior results from integrating microscopic interactions across spatial distributions rather than relying on pointwise constitutive assumptions. By contrast, traditional elastic models assume a direct, local connection between stress and strain, whereas our field-theoretic method captures complex behaviors such as microstructure and internal friction. Within this context, we formulate a nonlocal version of special relativistic elasticity by integrating constitutive equations within the field-theoretic structure. Subsequently, we extend these concepts into general relativity by building a corresponding field-theoretic model of nonlocal gravity through the nonlocalization of the gravitational field equations themselves.

Distributed Data Centers (DDDS) are essential for delivering high availability and low latency to end-users, utilizing Replicated Data Stores for these objectives. A core mechanism within these systems is the Consistent Ordered Vector Clock (COVS), which enables applications to retrieve data strictly according to their logical sequence. Nevertheless, current DDDS designs lack a unified, adaptable framework for integrating diverse, transactional, and query capabilities into their change operations. To bridge this gap, we present **Remove-Win**, a novel design for DFSs that resolves write-ordering and removal conflicts by applying the "remove-wins" paradigm. This framework supports diverse data structures by offering two key innovations: the **Remove-Win Tree (RWT)**, which ensures global removal order consistency across all nodes, and the **Remove-Win Dictionary (RWD)**, which maintains application-level ordering during value insertions and deletions. We evaluated RWT and RWD within the **RocksDB** environment against the standard Causal Tree. Results demonstrate that both new structures incur only a negligible performance cost relative to Causal Tree while significantly enhancing the success rate of change operations in distributed settings.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been highly successful in pinpointing genetic loci associated with human traits; however, identifying the specific causal genes and variants at these loci remains difficult. To address this challenge, we developed an integrated approach that combines GWAS data with a diverse array of functional genomic annotations. This method identifies genes by aggregating evidence from chromatin interactions, evolutionary conservation, gene expression, and regulatory element associations. By evaluating 18 traits—including body mass index, height, and educational attainment—we demonstrate that this strategy improves the precision of post-GWAS gene identification. Furthermore, leveraging trait-specific regulatory profiles derived from various genomic assays allows us to associate GWAS loci with genes more accurately than using a generic regulatory framework.

The nature of quiescent X-ray binaries in the galactic center is currently debated, hinging on whether transient neutron star systems have recurred too briefly for dust emission to re-radiate as infrared. Drawing on transient timing data and the standard model linking system age to recurrence intervals, we calculate that roughly 20\% of these transient neutron star systems should have recurred within 100,000 years. We propose this 1/f recurrence distribution as a practical method to estimate these timescales. Our analysis of 111 transient events in the galactic center region indicates a recurrence interval timescale of approximately 30,000 years. Consequently, we estimate that 21 neutron star X-ray binary transients remain too young to resolve the dust emission limitation central to the current argument.

The wide binary star test serves as a direct probe for modified gravity theories, offering direct observable predictions regarding a test particle's orbital period and semi-major axis. This study derives these theoretical period and semi-major axis predictions within the framework of modified gravity, specifically utilizing the generalized symmetric metric in conformally coupled scalar-tensor theories, which encompasses most such models. This specific theoretical setup allows for a direct comparison with recent Hubble Space Telescope findings on the orbital semi-major axes and periods of wide binary systems. The analysis indicates that the observational data strongly constrain these generalized scalar-tensor theories, with specific limits applicable to the test particle's orbital semi-major axis and period.

The stacking technique is a statistical approach used to analyze numerous radio sources sharing identical characteristics, such as their redshifts, while remaining elusive to individual detection. This study examines the physical properties of radio galaxies and sources at other ionizing luminosities across multiple redshifts by aggregating data from the ALFALFA survey. This study investigates fluid dynamics simulations of shocks generated by waves, with a specific application to the envelope of stellar eruptions. The analysis reveals that shocks induced by non-linear acoustic or p-mode waves result in substantial heating of the overlying material. Furthermore, when the heating rate surpasses a specific critical threshold, the formation of a "nascent" blastwave occurs within the flow. This new blastwave detaches from the source, propagates outward at supersonic velocities, and establishes a distinct contact discontinuity that effectively isolates the flow above it from the source region. The study derives an analytical expression for this critical heating rate, demonstrating that it bears a functional resemblance to the conditions defining the magnetic breakout of stars. In the context of planetary mass eruptions, such as those from red giants, the critical heating rate is typically exceeded by shocks, facilitating the development of nascent blastwaves. Conversely, in massive star envelopes, the required heating rate is often too high to be reached by standard shock events. Additionally, the research highlights that the presence of ambient magnetic fields can elevate the critical threshold, thereby impeding the genesis of the nascent blastwave phenomenon.

The Big Apple experiment, a proposed venture for the Next Generation European Muon Facility (nECMF), aims to conduct high-precision measurements of the electric and magnetic dipole moments of the nucleus of mercury-205 ($^{205}\textrm{Pb}$). This paper reviews the required advancements in accelerator technology, target design, and detection systems necessary for the Big Apple facility. It also examines the study of Big Apple anomalies, specifically focusing on implications for understanding astrophysical phenomena and the structure of nuclei.

We present a theoretical framework for integrating the atomic limit of a $d$-shell into the Dynamical Mean-Field Theory (DMFT) on the real-frequency axis. In this approach, the imaginary part of the Green's function is substituted with an atomic $d$-spectral function, while the Kramers-Kronig relations are applied to ensure the total Green's function remains exact within the atomic approximation. This method is applied to SrMnO$_3$, a system characterized by strong electron-electron interactions and significant hybridization between the Mn $3d$ and O $2p$ bands. The calculated optical conductivity aligns well with experimental data, and the agreement between the atomic limit and a full numerical solution of the Hamiltonian via the Exact Diagonalization Method (EDM) is found to be excellent. Furthermore, the results indicate that the proposed real-frequency axis approach is superior to the standard imaginary-frequency DMFT for both computational efficiency and precision.

We present an approach to enhance the stability of frequency-dependent phase shifts inherent in atomic qubit operations using the Mølmer-Sørensen scheme. This method employs balanced excitation and cooling of individual motional modes to generate a solvable model, from which we derive a global operation acting simultaneously on multiple quantum states. We demonstrate that this strategy significantly suppresses residual two-body errors caused by individual mode contributions. Furthermore, we introduce an optimized configuration utilizing the collective mode to further mitigate these stability limitations within the operation model. Finally, we illustrate the practical implementation of this technique in trapped-ion systems.

Although the pseudoprotoelectric perovskite family is renowned for its rich phase diagrams, compelling defects, and outstanding functional properties, a complete microscopic understanding of the mechanisms driving their diverse structural and non-local electronic behaviors remains elusive. Using a combination of machine learning, atomistic simulations, and high-resolution electron microscopy, we investigate a specific instance: the in-plane view of the microscopic incommensurate antiferroelectric pattern observed in a thin film of (Li,Sb)-doped BaTiO3. This study reveals a structural model composed of nanoscale regions of distinct ferroelectric polarizations that self-assemble into an intricate long-range incommensurate arrangement. We further demonstrate that high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) can effectively image the underlying electronic structure of this self-organized nanoscale pattern, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical atomic models and experimental observation.

We present predictions for the experimental observation of a novel, uncharted state of matter characterized as a three-dimensional (3D) correlated Dirac metal. This study employs a recently developed 4D generalization of the Hubbard–I approximation, utilizing it to anticipate the signatures of doped 3D correlated Dirac tetrahedrons within the pyrochlore lattice. Our results indicate that doping drives a transition from a correlated Dirac metal to a Mott insulator, a phase diagram feature that aligns with recent findings from neutron scattering experiments on $\text{Yb}_2\text{Ti}_2\text{O}_7$. Furthermore, the 4D Hubbard–I method accurately reproduces the energy spectrum of the four-component Dirac fluid observed in recent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) studies of the same material. Notably, the model forecasts a linear relationship between the energy scale of the correlated Dirac metal and the magnetic field scale of the corresponding spin system, a hypothesis that can be directly verified by future research.

Mixed models are frequently employed to analyze data characterized by two distinct response types, such as continuous measurements alongside categorical outcomes. While this approach is common, practitioners often struggle to identify the most suitable distribution for the joint likelihood, particularly regarding the component modeling the rate or proportion data. In this paper, we introduce a new multivariate framework designed to model both bimodal data sets. This method utilizes the multivariate $T$-distribution to achieve robustness against outliers in both the normal and inverse-Wishart structures. We demonstrate that our proposed approach is flexible and capable of handling various data configurations, catering to scenarios where data types may be combinations of rate/proportion and continuous/continuous, rate/proportion and categorical/categorical, continuous and categorical, or continuous and categorical. To illustrate the model's fit, we apply it to two real-world examples. Furthermore, we assess the model's robustness through a robustness analysis and evaluate its performance relative to competing methods via a simulation study. Finally, we evaluate the model's performance relative to competing methods through a simulation study.

Heavy Neutral Leptons (HNLs) are a compelling Heavy Neutrino candidate capable of explaining anomalies observed in lepton flavor universality and meson mixing. This study examines the feasibility of accessing the eMeV mass-scale of HNLs through increased sensitivity to $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, utilizing the upcoming NA62 experiment. We estimate the capabilities of the upgraded setup to achieve a 100,000-fold improvement in sample size for $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays, resulting in the first experimental limits on HNLs in the eMeV mass range. Future constraints from this process and its charge-conjugate counterpart, $K^- \to \pi^0 e^- N$, could potentially probe total mixing angles $|U_{eN}|^2$ as low as $10^{-14}$ for 200 MeV HNLs. Additionally, we investigate the complementarity of this search with existing limits from LHC mono-lepton analyses and results from MEG II regarding the transition $\mu \to e N$.

We examine the spectral shifts observed within a rotating ring interferometer, comparing the frequency of a beam traveling clockwise versus one traveling counter-clockwise as measured from a Galilean reference frame. In this analysis, the concept of a "quasi-Photon" is introduced to account for the Doppler effect arising from the motion of the mirrors relative to this frame. The paper further investigates potential $\Lambda$-type anomalies in the spectrum and concludes that, within a strictly physical and non-idealized setting, such theoretical $\Lambda$-anomalies do not materialize.

This work examines the parabolic adjoint operation associated with a Borel subgroup $B$ relative to a Borel-subgroup-compatible parabolic structure $(B,P)$ in classical type $A$. Leveraging a previously established theory of Weierstrass sections for nilpotent orbits under nilpotent parabolics developed in the authors' companion piece ("Weierstrass sections... in Type $A$"), we identify and describe the nilfibre corresponding to this parabolic operation. Our descriptions of this nilfibre carry significant implications for the study of nilfibre cells within nilflagmann variety strata, as well as the nilvarieties themselves. In the specific instance of type $A_2$, we utilize these descriptions to offer a refined, explicit characterization of the components comprising the nilfibre.

Although neural language models (LMs) have largely replaced $N$ -gram models due to their superior accuracy, the lack of theoretical support for integrating them with existing $N$ -gram systems has hindered progress. In this study, we introduce a theoretical framework that establishes the theoretical connection between the theoretical distribution of neural LM$s$ and the empirical $N$ -gram distribution, demonstrating that the residual training of $N$ -grams using neural methods can be understood as refining the empirical $N$ -gram distribution. We further introduce a modified Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) criterion to determine the optimal $N$ -gram order $K$ when training $N$ -grams using neural residuals. Experiments on the Common Crawl Wikipedia dataset indicate that this approach yields an improved $N$ -gram model that surpasses standard neural-only models.

Given a Laurent series $f \in k((t))$ with coefficients in a field of characteristic zero, the Laurent series inversion performs $\Kogaku$-potential reduction on the space of non-compact GKKP invariants of F-groove categories. We demonstrate that this result extends to certain classes of power series $f \in k[[t]]$, particularly those arising from the analytic uniformization of $\mathbb Q$-gembian varieties. In each scenario, the computation preserves the volume invariant.

Accurately reconstructing uncooperative face shapes remains a significant challenge in 3D dense face alignment, primarily due to extreme variations in pose and poor image quality. This paper introduces a novel 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction system, termed **SAADRnet** (Self-Alanced Dual Face Regression Networks), which processes images in an anti-aligned dual-stream configuration. The approach first employs an anchor-based selection mechanism to identify the optimal pose range, subsequently dividing the input image into an upper and lower stream. This strategy facilitates an initial rough alignment of the top and bottom face halves, followed by iterative optimization to achieve precise and stable reconstruction. Furthermore, an integrated mechanism is implemented to mitigate the mutual adverse influence between these streams. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that SAADRnet surpasses existing methods across a broad spectrum of benchmarks spanning twelve different databases.

This study examines the behavior of fractons within efficient (low-energy) theories used to describe the fractonic Higgs mechanism, which occurs when translational symmetry breaks spontaneously. These low-dimensional theories enable a closer analysis of fracton properties beyond their large-distance limits. As a specific example, an efficient theory exploring how translational symmetry breaks efficiently is developed in three spatial dimensions (3+1 spacetime dimensions). This model demonstrates that a specific type of fracton, termed a "plecton," appears in such scenarios. The term "plecton" is suggested because this plechon exhibits similarities to both electric charges in the standard (conventional) lattice Higgs model and to Isanyons in the toric code. The study further establishes a correspondence between the torsion of the underlying toric code and the statistical property (statistics) of the resulting plechon. Additionally, it is proven that the type of plechon formed is contingent upon the type of torsion present in the parent toric code structure.

We examine if the emergence of density fluctuations in the $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, resulting from the partial collapse of causality within primordial disturbances, can generate populations of primordial black holes. This analysis focuses specifically on the single-field scenario involving the exponential potential. We establish that this mechanism is viable for generating PBHs within certain regions of the parameter space, with the resulting black hole masses reaching up to approximately $10^{17}$ g. Furthermore, we determine the fraction of the universal fraction of PBH formation in these conditions. We also assess several observational constraints, including those regarding the cosmic microwave background anisotropies, the stochastic gravitational wave background, the abundance of accreted PBHs, and the cosmic isotope composition, to establish the allowed intervals for the PBH mass function.

We introduce the class of marked ordered trees, comprising all ordered trees where each vertex carries a positive integer label. Our objective is to investigate the joint distribution of tree size, the count of edges connecting vertices labeled $a$ and $b$, and the depth of the most deeply occurring vertex labeled $a$. Additionally, we examine an enhanced model involving coins placed on vertices; this allows us to determine the distribution related to the height of the highest path containing exactly $k$ heads. Our approach utilizes recursive constructions and a bijection to 2-Dyck paths, with asymptotic behavior analyzed via analytic combinatorics in several variables. As a result, we identify 2-Dyck paths as the optimal encoding for these structures, enabling the application of Diophantine approximation techniques to derive asymptotics. Complementing this, our recursive framework facilitates the derivation of difference equations, which we leverage to explicitly calculate moments and the correlation between the specified quantities and the tree's size.

This investigation seeks to assess the efficacy of Intelligible Optical Character Recognition (iOCR), an Information-enhanced OCR technique, in extracting data from paper ballots for election tallies. By integrating information about expected columnar data patterns, iOCR aims to produce reliable character identification even when encountering unfamiliar fonts, languages, or noisy image contexts. To test iOCR's performance, we employed the Danet et al. (2018) dataset, which includes ballots from 11 distinct U.S. states, along with supplementary ballot collections gathered from various municipalities in Colorado. Our findings indicate that iOCR excels at accurately identifying names of ballot measures and office-seekers, significantly outperforming standard OCR methods, especially regarding noisy scans. Furthermore, these results suggest that such technology could enable volunteers to automate vote tabulation, thereby alleviating the substantial manual labor currently required for counting paper ballots.

Recent advancements in time series analysis highlight the potential of wide neural networks, even when over-parameterized to the extent of overfitting training data. This study investigates the fitting capabilities of such networks within a linear time series setting, specifically examining a regression setup where linear auto-regressive (AR) coefficients are learned by an AR network. Although only linear architectures are modeled here, they serve as a fundamental basis for more intricate representations; for instance, a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) capable of approximating any function $f$ can reconstruct an AR structure by sequentially mapping inputs $x_1, \dots, x_d$ to intermediate states $z_1, \dots, z_d$ before producing an output $f(z_d)$, given appropriate input mappings $g_i$. The theoretical results indicate that despite the capacity to memorize noise in the linear AR framework, wide networks retain strong generalization performance. Specifically, if $d$ denotes the number of lagged inputs and the number of training examples $n$ is at least $d$, zero training error is associated with an empirical risk minimizer that yields a test loss of order $\frac{d}{n} + \lambda$. This value represents the statistical noise term $\lambda$, contrasting sharply with the standard high-dimensional machine learning regime—where feature count far exceeds sample size ($d \gg n$)—in which linear predictability typically collapses and test loss becomes unbounded at $\lambda = \infty$. Speech enhancement serves as a fundamental technology in numerous applications, including automatic speech recognition, virtual reality, and teleconferencing. Its primary function is to eliminate or mitigate adverse impacts from background noise, thereby improving audio quality for these uses. This study introduces a novel deep learning architecture for single-channel speech enhancement that utilizes full attention mechanisms to process inputs with a complete bidirectional flow. The proposed model was evaluated on the RASPER dataset, where it achieved superior performance when compared to other leading deep learning-based methods.

Music festivals attract attendees from across the globe, fostering a unique convergence of individuals that creates an ideal environment for pathogens to spread. However, little research has examined how the social interactions at these events facilitate infectious disease transmission. This paper investigates the epidemiological risks associated with major festivals, utilizing data from Ozzfest 2010 to examine the mobility patterns of its attendees. By reconstructing the contact networks derived from this movement data, we applied an SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) model to explore viral transmission scenarios. Our findings reveal that introducing a single infected individual into the network could theoretically infect over 1,000 other attendees. Consequently, festival organizers must prioritize public health measures to mitigate these substantial transmission risks.

This study examines a dynamic pricing model for storage services, specifically analyzing the optimal, self-imposed risk management strategies for storage providers. The framework highlights how risk-averse operators can establish and enforce risk restrictions to stabilize pricing fluctuations and mitigate market volatility. Influenced by these internal risk controls, the resulting market equilibrium evolves into a Markovian solution characterized by a hysteresis loop, reflecting the system's path dependence. Furthermore, the research investigates how risk allocation mechanisms affect pricing stability and offers insights into the most effective risk allocation methods for optimizing storage markets.

The generation of ultrafast electron dynamics, particularly through the interference of coherent processes occurring on the attosecond timescale, represents a central objective in contemporary research within strong field physics. Although recent advancements have enabled the observation of coherent dynamics during coherent Coulombian excitation and coherent supercyclic reactions, significant hurdles remain in achieving similar control for complex multi-body systems, such as those involving multiple electrons. This study presents the generation of coherent coherent electron dynamics in the context of the three-electron K-L-M Auger decay following inner-shell X-ray excitation of an atomic target. By utilizing circularly polarized X-rays to induce coherent electron dynamics in the context of the three-electron K-L-M Auger decay following monochromatic X-ray excitation of an atomic target, we demonstrate that varying the helicity of the incident circularly polarized X-rays allows for selective manipulation of coherent electron dynamics. We employed two Global Climate Models (GCMs) with simplified physics to examine and contrast atmospheric circulation patterns across the full spectrum from geostrophic turbulence to equatorial super-rotation. Using different sets of parameters for planetary albedo and surface thermal emission, we established a regime diagram characterized by distinct circulation regimes. In both models, the transition from super-rotation to turbulence occurred unilaterally as a function of albedo, whereas the base levels of circulation intensity depended on the specific thermal physics applied. Notably, both simulations produced a regime of western hemisphere Hadley cells that span the entire hemisphere under specific parameter conditions, a state we identify as an analog to geostrophic turbulence.

Initial model weights are crucial for deep learning performance, and while industry practices often rely on models pre-trained on massive datasets like ImageNet, these assets are finite. As new data becomes inaccessible, researchers must generate synthetic alternatives, yet current methods fail to match ImageNet's scale, diversity, and realism. This gap significantly hinders overall task performance. Addressing these challenges, we introduce Stochastic Differential Data (SD3), a framework capable of synthesizing vast, varied, and photorealistic images at the scale of ImageNet. Our approach builds on the theory of stochastic processes, utilizing score diffusion models trained on limited seed datasets to generate target distributions through stochastic interpolation. Complementing this, we propose a new curriculum strategy that dynamically adjusts the proportion of training data in response to the stochastic complexity of the target distribution. By integrating high-fidelity data from state-of-the-art diffusion generators with seed information under a stochastic curriculum, our method achieves a significant breakthrough: models trained on our synthesized data surpass pre-trained ImageNet benchmarks by up to $6.3\%$ on various tasks, including those involving video generation and language-image interaction.

This study explores the fundamental nature of algebraic multiplicity, establishing novel connections between characteristic polynomials, the zeta functions of quiver representations, and the characteristic ideals of non-commutative rings. While prior research by various authors has focused on determining the algebraic multiplicity of a matrix $A$ through the characteristic polynomial $\chi_A(t)=\det(tI-A)$, this paper introduces a completely different computational framework. Specifically, it demonstrates that this multiplicity can be derived from the zeta function associated with the quiver representations of the path algebra $k\langle x,y\rangle / \langle yx-x^2y\rangle$. Furthermore, the work presents a new formula for this multiplicity in terms of the zeta function of the matrix commutator subgroup. The core methodology relies on the theory of invariant theory.

We examine pairwise generation of photons from the bimodal vacuum state of a parapositronium atom interacting with an optical resonator, where the "atoms" are composed of ensembles of cavity-coupled quantum dots engineered to possess effective long-lived dipole moments. Pairing correlations are analyzed using the Stochastic Master Equation formalism, considering both resonant and off-resonant coupling of the dipole to the cavity mode, with a specific focus on optimizing optical interferometric phase sensitivity. We further investigate the generation of quantum squeezing within these bimodal states. We demonstrate that highly squeezed states emerge when the quantum dot ensemble is detuned from the cavity resonance, enabling precision phase measurements exceeding the standard quantum limit.

Donor spins in silicon are a leading candidate for quantum computing, yet their scalability is constrained by a limited number of controllable defects. Recent advancements have successfully coupled two donors to create a qubit with a significantly extended coherence time, and current efforts are focused on determining the optimal three- or multi-donor configurations. To guide these experiments, we simulate the comprehensive wavefunctions of two- and three-donor systems within this paper. By employing a multi-valley effective mass approach, we determine the donor electron ground state, which involves electrons occupying two degenerate valleys. Our analysis reveals that exchange interactions, which are essential for both quantum communication among donors and donor-based two-qubit gates, scale linearly with the parallel displacement of donors relative to the crystallographic axes. Furthermore, we identify specific donor alignments in the third valley location that maximize exchange coupling, achieving interaction energies up to approximately 100 $\mu$eV in paired donors and 1000 $\mu$eVs in triplet donor configurations.

V2X communications have emerged as a key technology for enabling intelligent transportation systems (ITS) by facilitating data exchange between vehicles and their surroundings. This study introduces a cooperative Non-Orthogonal Multiple Access (NOMA) scheme designed to support cooperative awareness functions within an ITS framework. Specifically, this protocol allows a cooperative transmitter to assist two geographically distant and spatially multiplexed receivers, addressing a scenario that is otherwise unfeasible using conventional power allocation methods. This paper analytically derives closed-form expressions for both the outage probability and the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the cooperative transmit signal's power at road intersections—a location selected due to heightened accident risks. Numerical results confirm that the proposed theoretical framework accurately reflects the proposed protocol's performance. Furthermore, these simulations demonstrate that adaptive cooperative NOMA outperforms conventional NOMA, particularly within congested road intersections.

This study introduces a novel non-cooperative game model designed to address the limitations of existing static TDD pattern scheduling approaches. Recognizing the insufficiency of prior methods due to their rigidity, this research focuses on optimizing TDD patterns dynamically to adapt to varying traffic loads across cell types. The proposed game model allows both cell operators and the network operator to submit their individual traffic requirements as bids, enabling the base station to select the most suitable pattern based on these inputs and subsequent payoffs. Analysis shows that the resulting game possesses a structure supporting a unique Nash Equilibrium, which is achieved through iterative bidding updates. Furthermore, we demonstrate that at this equilibrium state, the network achieves its maximum utility. In terms of performance, simulation results indicate that this proposed dynamic scheduling method significantly improves system throughput and reduces unmet traffic demand compared to traditional static scheduling strategies.

A theoretical model is introduced to examine how a Hall anomaly, previously unexplained, arises from vacancies within a rigid lattice of vortex tubes. This anomaly was observed in zero-field cooling experiments on BSCCO thin films with a (110) crystal orientation and a current flowing along the [001] direction; notably, a magnetic field applied parallel to both the vortex tubes and the Hall electric field triggers this anomaly. Our findings indicate that the model accurately predicts the anomaly's origin: thermally induced movement of vortex tubes creates vacancies in their fixed lattice, and a magnetic field parallel to the tubes magnifies this effect by influencing vacancy dynamics related to the Mott mechanism. Furthermore, the model successfully accounts for the specific features of the experimental data, including the Hall anomaly's nonlinearity, magnetic field dependence, and the fourfold symmetry of the critical field exhibiting a local maximum. As a result, this framework offers a theoretical explanation for previously unresolved experimental results regarding the Hall anomaly in these systems.

In this region, we calculate the first- and second-order moments of these systems and observe that they exhibit fixed-point behavior indicative of the (N=1) matrix random-singularity ensembles at the critical points $m=1,2$. Furthermore, we observe that the second-order moment values at the critical points $m=1,2$ align closely with the second-order moment values of the (N=1) matrix random-singularity enasures at the same critical points $m=1,2$.

We demonstrate that finite-dimensional commuting squares of von Neumann algebras, where two factors produce a subfactor of finite index, are fully characterized by three specific numerical invariants. Furthermore, an explicit construction based on these invariants is provided that guarantees the resulting conjugacy class of the subfactor produced is of finite depth.

This study introduces a novel neural network architecture, termed the Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN), designed to learn ordinary differential equations (ODEs) while preserving the symplectic geometric structure inherent in their flow. Symplecticity conservation confers substantial benefits, including long-term stability and accurate trajectory prediction over extended durations. We demonstrate through both numerical experiments and real-world applications that this method outstrips current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, leveraging this persistent stability, our approach effectively captures physical dynamics, making it ideally suited for tasks like derivative forecasting in financial modeling. Finally, we validate the model's flexibility by successfully adapting it to various non-Hamiltonian ODE scenarios.

Enhancing trust in deep learning models is increasingly vital, particularly regarding their robustness against adversarial inputs. While prior research focused on detecting and classifying such attacks, this paper shifts focus to preventing them. We propose a novel trustable model that integrates human feedback loops to generate trusted scores and expand datasets. Specifically, our approach filters out malicious inputs to exclude them from training, while simultaneously using trusted scores to refine the confidence levels of predictions made by the underlying neural network. By simultaneously expanding the dataset with these protected examples and refining the confidence levels of predictions made by the underlying neural network. We evaluate our method on the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in both robustness against various attacks and overall accuracy.

Detecting contraband via automatic x-ray security scanners is widely recognized as a highly effective method for prohibiting dangerous items. Despite this utility, the domain remains significantly under-explored, primarily due to the scarcity of well-annotated datasets and the lack of specialized research dedicated to it. This study introduces a novel, comprehensive, and high-quality dataset comprising 107 prohibited objects arranged in realistic packing scenarios, resulting in 100k annotated images. This collection surpasses existing benchmarks by offering a broader spectrum of contraband categories, higher image resolution, and diverse viewing angles. Furthermore, the intricate overlapping of objects in these scans creates complex intrusions that pose substantial detection challenges. To address these specific difficulties, we propose a Lateral Inhibition (LI) Module designed to mitigate false alarms caused by mutual occlusions and background interference. Evaluations on the new dataset reveal that incorporating this LI module yields a 5.6% improvement in the mIoU metric compared to a baseline model. Finally, we establish a robust foundation for future research by releasing the data and associated code publicly.

Word sense disambiguation (WSD) serves as a foundational task in natural language processing aimed at identifying the appropriate word meaning within a specific context. This study introduces a new WSD framework built upon a dual-listing word sense model (DL-WSM), which integrates multiple aspects of surrounding context and utilizes a comprehensive gloss for each sense. We developed a context-gloss improvement module that refines the standard definitions by fusing them with surrounding sentence context, thereby offering clearer semantic distinctions and enhancing overall performance. We implemented this proposed DL-WSM model within the proposed framework using the SenseEval-1 dataset for evaluation. Experiments demonstrate superior results compared to other state-of-the-art approaches using the same benchmark dataset.

This study derives an integral representation for $\frac{1}{\Gamma(z)}$ employing regularization techniques, which is valid throughout the complex plane. Our approach involves factor out $-z$ from the argument of the Gamma function to utilize an existing integral formulation defined on $\mathbb{R}^+$, thereby establishing a regularized expression claimed to be the most accessible of its kind. Using this formulation, we derive several associated properties and integral formulas. Additionally, we introduce a new regularization representation and compare it against existing formulations in the literature.

This study presents an investigation into top quark production within proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing inelastic p+p collisions as a reference framework. The analysis relies on factorization theorems, which permit the extraction of the top-quark fragmentation function from p+p data and the nuclear top-quark parton distribution function (nCTeqp) from proton-lead (p+Pb) production cross-sections. The input nPDF distribution is constrained by a global fit incorporating various processes, most notably semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering (SIDIS), D-meson cross-sections, and jet production, alongside the relevant $\ppb$ and hadron-helicity configurations.

The research focuses on two primary observables: the top-quark transverse momentum ($t_p$) and the top-quark rapidity ($y_t$). The $t_p$ spectrum is examined through the probability distribution function $P(t_p)$, while the $y_t$ spectrum is analyzed in terms of the nuclear modification factor ($R_{AA}$). The study employs the nCTeqp distribution to simulate p+Pb collisions, comparing the results against experimental data obtained from the CERN LHC. The analysis incorporates the effects of nuclear shadowing, partonic energy loss, and the nuclear medium on the final state.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL interpretation involves translating natural language queries into database SQL statements, serving as a fundamental tool for database semantics. Although most existing works concentrate on this area, the leading approach utilizing neural end-to-end mappings struggles with two key issues: (1) the excessive generation of irrelevant database schema columns and (2) the scarcity of schema-centric training objectives. This paper introduces a schema-assisted cross-domain text-to-SQL interpretation framework designed to mitigate these limitations. We implement a joint modeling strategy that jointly predicts schema elements—specificity including attribute values and value schemas—alongside SQL outputs. Empirical results demonstrate significant improvements in both SQL execution accuracy and schema element prediction accuracy over baseline models.

This paper examines the field of privacy-preserving machine learning for networking data, highlighting both current methods and open challenges through a survey organized by specific learning model types. We highlight linear models, including those utilizing the $\text{SGD}$ framework, as well as advanced approaches such as federated learning and heterogeneous learning. Furthermore, we explore privacy mechanisms tailored for tree-based models, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and contrastive learning. Additionally, we outline significant challenges and potential avenues for research within this area of differential privacy.

Following a decade of operations, the launch of the Euclid Space mission is poised to significantly advance our understanding of the cosmos, with the full potential of its capabilities expected to be realized only through extensive data analysis. We introduce a hybrid phase-space hydrodynamic approach that integrates hydrodynamics with the positive phase-space representation of quantum fluids, yielding locally coupled, coarse-grained Euler equations for interacting Bose gases. This method addresses short- and long-range correlation effects separately: it models density and energy through quantum hydrodynamics (capturing long-range correlations), while utilizing the positive phase-space formalism to incorporate other integrated condensate properties that encode short-range correlations. This distinction proves especially valuable for systems like the interacting 1D Lieb-Liniger gas, where standard mean-field quantum Euler equations—based on density and only a single parameter describing short-range behavior—often break down. Our model employs two interacting fluid velocities (from the density and phase of the positive phase-space forms) to construct a closed Eulerian system. When reduced to a low-speed limit, this framework generates a quantum hydrodynamic equation resembling the modified Gross-Pitaevsky-Hartree-Fock system for non-condensate gases. Furthermore, applying our quantum hydrodynamic equations to a quantum turbulent 1D Lieb-Liniger gas allows the calculation of effective quantum fluids characterized by new velocity and modified interacting densities.

Temporal action detection (TAD) involves identifying the onset and offset of actions within a video, and it has attracted significant research attention. Although current methods have achieved notable results, they still contend with two primary obstacles: the availability of precise annotation data and the efficient integration of temporal and contextual information for detection. Addressed to mitigate these challenges is Dual-Context Action Network (DCAN), which operates in a two-stage framework. In the first phase, DCAN employs a series of temporal action detectors (TADs) anchored at sliding segments of specific, predefined keys; this stage leverages a robust temporal network designed to maximize performance in isolation given limited supervisory signals. During the second phase, DCAN refines the outcomes from stage one using an advanced detection head that simultaneously synthesizes precise prior knowledge and dual contexts—specificating semantic information and temporal structure—to achieve enhanced accuracy. It is worth noting that DCAN functions as a plug-and-play architecture compatible with various backbone networks. Experimental evaluations on two prominent benchmarks, ActivityNet v1.3 and Kinetics v10, confirm that DCAN surpasses the state-of-the-art, delivering superior performance even when utilizing simplified backbones.

Significant fluctuations at the ion temperature gradient (ITG) frequency range, identified as "palm tree modes," were observed in the JET tokamak during a specific H-mode discharge. These features manifested as distinct structures within the core of a bright E×B shear-suppressed pedestal and extended into the mid-radius region. Neutron radiography revealed these modes to be toroidally elongated with a poloidal wavelength of approximately 10 cm, a scale comparable to the local poloidal aspect ratio. These structures exhibited strong radial migration, moving outward in correlation with fluctuations in the plasma current. While their exact origin remains debated, two primary hypotheses exist: they could be localized, large-scale ITG turbulence or poloidal breech instabilities resulting from magnetic well perturbations caused by neutral beam injection (NBI). Analysis of the fluctuation wavenumber spectrum supports the first hypothesis, indicating a dominant toroidal mode number of n=10. Furthermore, the dependence of these modes on plasma current aligns with expectations for ITG turbulence, specifically regarding the parallel wavenumber ($k_{||}$) and the safety factor ($q$). Consequently, these results provide support for interpreting the "palm tree modes" as ITG in nature.

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has garnered significant attention for its potential in wireless networks, and this paper investigates IRS-assisted radar systems to assess their ability to estimate target parameters. The IRS configures the diagonal phase shifts of its passive reflecting elements to optimize and subsequently improve target parameter accuracy. Building on a derived joint transmit and IRS precoding framework, the study addresses three core parameter estimation tasks: range estimation, velocity estimation, and direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation. Specifically, the objective is to maximize the diagonal entries of the sparse covariance matrix by adjusting both the radar's transmit precoding and the IRS precoding. Since this optimization problem is non-convex, the authors first simplify it into a manageable form and then solve the resulting sub-problems iteratively. Numerical simulations confirm the efficacy of the proposed approach, demonstrating performance gains of up to 1.6 dB compared to existing baseline methods.

Fuzzing serves as a primary method for uncovering security flaws in software, yet determining the effectiveness of individual fuzzers remains difficult. This paper introduces a methodology to evaluate and contrast fuzzer performance by measuring their behavioral output. The proposed approach injects carefully crafted inputs containing specific behaviors, allowing funder processing to manifest as observable system events—such as instruction count variations, memory access patterns, or system call frequencies. By analyzing how different fuzzers react to these inputs through observation of these metrics, we can assess and compare their capabilities. We tested the framework using three widely used funder implementations, demonstrating that this approach successfully identifies performance differences and offers valuable insights for enhancing future fuzzing strategies.

Although pretrained models are commonly used in continual learning, this study establishes a rigorous baseline by developing a systematic framework that controls for confounding variables. The researchers attribute the baseline's strong results to the difficulty of the experimental setup, which masks the negative effects of typical continual learning algorithms, such as excessive smoothing or redundant rehearsal. By providing this robust benchmark, the work facilitates a cleaner comparison of future continual learning techniques.

This paper investigates the query complexity required to find an $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium in two-player Lipschitz games, where the player sets are metric spaces and the loss functions are $\lambda$-Lipschitz across all directions. Deep neural networks have established themselves as the leading choice for a wide range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. We report the detection of photon recoil phenomena in the photon absorption, momentum transfer, and temperature reduction of an ultracold ^{88}\text{Sr} vapor using a single laser beam. Discontinuous shear thickening (DST), a phenomenon where suspending solids in a liquid causes a sudden rise in viscosity under specific stress levels, has long fascinated researchers. This review examines recent theoretical advancements and experimental findings that explore the universal features of DST, beginning with the macroscopic and microscopic traits of the transition, followed by the application of DST in various fields, and concluding with a synthesis of current theories regarding this complex behavior.

This study introduces a motion-corrected, free-breathing 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequence designed for capturing respiration dynamics in three dimensions plus temporal resolution ("3D+T") without interrupting breathing. The proposed workflow utilizes a low-resolution, low-specific absorption rate (SAR) 4D key-respiration (key-respiration) scan to generate a predictive respiration model via machine learning. Subsequently, a high-resolution, high-SAR, free-breathing 4D T2-weighted TSE sequence is executed, with its data sorted and corrected using the forecasted respiration curve to yield a motion-corrected, free-breathing, high-resolution 4D T2-weighted TSE sequence. The sorting strategy divides the high-resolution scan into multiple static acquisitions triggered by time, with the duration of each segment modulated according to the real-time respiration prediction. The resulting motion-corrected sequences are reconstructed using a combination of a combinatorial optimization algorithm and a Bloch simulation-based cost function. Validation was performed on a healthy male subject, demonstrating that the method successfully generated motion-corrected, free-breathing, high-resolution 4D T2-weighted TSE data.

This paper introduces a secure control synthesis technique for nonlinear systems with input constraints operating in an environment containing unknown but bounded disturbances. The proposed feedback controller guarantees that the state trajectory remains within a specified safe set despite these disturbances, representing a generalization of Input Constrained Control Barrier Functions. The proposed approach is demonstrated in a case study involving a robotic arm tasked with maintaining contact with an obstacle.

This study introduces a straightforward method for deriving precise paired-permutation p-values under arbitrary dependency structures by leveraging the concept of coupling. This study introduces a comprehensive, harmonized dataset covering the global shipping industry from 1966 to 2019, encompassing freight rates, shipping volumes, prices for new vessels, secondhand transactions, and ship scrap. We detail the construction methodology for each variable and the specific criteria applied to filter and align the data, ultimately providing complete statistical descriptions of the entire series as well as the individual components.

This paper extends the concept of loom areas, originally defined by the authors in collaboration with M. Thurston on triangulations of loom surfaces. We demonstrate that these extended loom surfaces carry a natural geometric structure resembling a veering triangulation. Furthermore, we establish a constructive procedure to transform any triangled loom surface into a specific type of surface known as a "monodrom loom surface." This process ensures that the resulting monodrom variant preserves both the area and the associated twisting number found in the initial triangled form. In our context, triangled loom surfaces serve as a broader generalization suitable for various three-body configurations, including those exhibiting chaotic behavior.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in analyzing structured data and have become prevalent in the last few years. A primary driver for this popularity is the ability of GNNs to implicitly learn aggregations from graph-structured inputs, which inherently yields structural interpretability. Despite this, the learned neighbor aggregation weights for graph edges remain opaque, hindering a deeper understanding of the graph's learned representations. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that trains GNNs to induce a sparse pattern of edge weights, thereby creating more comprehensible models. Our method relies on a specific property of GNN message-passing mechanisms: the interpretation of an edge weight as the weighted sum of messages across all message-passing layers. We demonstrate theoretically that our approach is compatible with various popular GNN architectures. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that our technique successfully interprets complex GNN behaviors while maintaining competitive performance.

CountSketch serves as a space-efficient method for estimating high-dimensional vector properties, such as $\ell_2$ norms and orthogonality, and remains one of the most popular choices for large-scale data processing. Previous research demonstrated that even with just $O(\log d)$ rows, CountSketch achieves constant approximation factors; however, these methods assumed non-adaptive input conditions where all entries were known in advance. This work investigates the performance of CountSketch when an adversary adaptively selects entries to maximize the algorithm's error. We establish tight bounds for the adaptive setting, proving that while CountSketch retains constant-factor approximation abilities, it requires $O(\sqrt{\log d})$ rows to do so—an additional factor of $\sqrt{\log d}$ compared to non-adaptive conditions. In contrast, we show that simple $\text{TailMinSketch}$ fails to provide even a constant approximation with non-zero failure probability in this adaptive context, necessitating more sophisticated techniques like CountSketch to handle adaptive adversaries. Practical experiments confirm these theoretical findings.

Anderson, which was developed in his seminal paper on the structure of such spaces. Furthermore, this part establishes several fundamental properties of the post-surgery metric. These insights pave the way for Part III, where we will derive the corresponding scalar curvature splitting theorem analogous to Anderson's structure theorem for these manifolds.

When a type-II superconductor rotates in a magnetic field parallel to its axis, vortices translate linearly; when the field is tilted, the vortices experience both translation and rotation. This paradigm shift allows us to examine superconducting vortex liquids through the lens of relativistic hydrodynamics. In this context, the moving vortices function analogously to a fluid with specific entropy, rendering the vortices themselves the carrier of this entropy. We concentrate specifically on the transverse Nernst effect—where uniform movement of vortices generates a thermal flow perpendicular to that motion—and analyze how fluid dissipation influences this phenomenon across two distinct scenarios: a fully dissipative Landau vortex state and a weakly dissipative vorticeson VLE.

This paper introduces a novel predictive control framework designed to address the practical challenges of learning-based approaches, specifically their data requirements and poor generalization. Key innovations include a predictive model trained on historical system data to estimate aggregate flexibility and the utilization of Model Predictive Control (MPC) to incorporate learned model errors. Evaluations across two distinct use cases demonstrate that this method achieves performance on par with MPC systems enhanced by reinforcement learning, while significantly outperforming standard MPC in terms of adaptability and robustness.

This study introduces a novel framework for predicting future stock prices by integrating the BERT andGAN approaches. BERT's capability to capture the nuanced semantic and syntactic structures within financial reports makes it an ideal choice for preprocessing and extracting features, which are subsequently utilized by a Conditional GAN (CGAN). The CGAN leverages these high-caliber features to generate precise forecast values. We evaluated the model using the S&P 500 index dataset, focusing on predicting the closing prices of S&P 500 constituent companies. Our findings reveal that the proposed model achieves superior predictive accuracy and outperforms existing methods, thereby validating the efficacy of combining BERT and CGAN for stock price forecasting tasks.

Envelope formalism serves as an essential framework for analyzing nonlinear mixing processes, such as parametric amplification and scattering, within systems like optoelectronics and high-energy physics. It functions by decoupling slow evolution equations from fast oscillatory components. This study introduces a distinct set of universal envelope equations that describe the dynamics of all-microscopic scattering processes, encompassing optoelectronic and high-energy instances alike, which are characterized by microscopic energy exchanges and subsequent net changes. In optoelectronics, this net effect occurs when light interacts with an electric field to produce another photon, whereas in high-energy physics it involves collisions between particles resulting in different outgoing particles. Representing the system through a Hamiltonian, the proposed formalism employs a specific transformation to derive equations governing the separation of scattering into rapid phases and slow amplitudes. Its validity across both domains is underscored by an examination of optoelectronic cases, notably degenerate and non-degenerate parametric processes as well as single- and two-photon optical nonlinearities, alongside parametric generation and scattering in particle systems. Furthermore, within high-energy contexts, this formalism is applied to illustrate how particle interactions are described by a Lagrangian, yielding a theory of general parametric processes for particle optics.

This study examines double Higgs boson production in future high-luminosity $pp$ and high-energy $pp$ colliders, focusing on scenarios where the Higgs sector is extended. We employ an Effective Field Theory (EFT) to probe potential Beyond Standard Model (BSM) contributions to Higgs self-couplings, utilizing the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) within the Higgs basis parameterization. Our analysis utilizes projected collider scales of 35 TeV for the HL-LHC and 100 TeV for FCC-hh. Complementarily, we explore the determination of the triple-Higgs coupling $g_{hhh}$ through doubly resonant Higgs boson production ($pp \to hh$) at proposed high-energy $pp$ facilities like FCC-ee and CLIC operating at 100 TeV. Additionally, we project the reach of the SMEFT coefficient $g_{\lambda\lambda}$ for various new physics scales ($\Lambda$) associated with triple-Higgs interactions.

We construct a family of gravity Lagrangians parameterized by arbitrary functions, which generalize the Einstein-Hilbert action. Our analysis reveals that the field equations corresponding to these Lagrangians are satisfied identically due to the diffeomorphism invariance of the action, a consequence of specific mathematical identities. Consequently, the Einstein tensor acquires additional contributions from our parametrization, yet the core geometric structure remains anchored by differential-geometric identities rather than independent dynamical rules. We suspect that higher-order terms in non-cinetic gravity share this characteristic; thus, Lagrangians with such terms might lack the physical content found in the standard Einstein-Hilbert formulation.

We present a methodology for analyzing collisions between two localized shocks in a five-dimensional asymptotically anti-de Sitter ($\mathcal{N}=4$ Super Yang-Mills theory) that extends beyond the leading order in central density. By employing a series expansion framework grounded in transverse density variations, we detail the computational approach for higher-density corrections. As a practical application, we calculate second-density order outcomes for shocks with transverse profiles mirroring those found in nucleon-nucleon collisions, finding that while the leading density density remains unchanged, the subsequent higher-density orders are significantly altered. We also examine the formation of the final state's thermalized quark-gluon plasma, specifically examining the expansion and hadronization phases. Our results indicate that the initial density distribution persists throughout the system's evolution, a trait that could potentially be utilized to reconstruct the initial collision conditions from final-state hadron distributions.

Long-standing theories propose that intense star formation generates outflows capable of regulating further stellar activity within host galaxies. While current capabilities exist to detect these features in localized regions, the necessity for future instruments remains to map them continuously across entire disks. To address this gap, we introduce DUVEtT, a novel emission-line catalog derived from the MUSE data from the MUSE Deep Evolutionary Snapshot Survey (MUSE-DES). Utilizing DUVEetT, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of star-forming galaxies (SFGs) and active galactic nuclei (AGN) to evaluate the prevalence of outflows in the cosmic present. Our findings reveal that a vast majority of SFGs exhibit outflows, with the phenomenon being even more ubiquitous in starburst systems. Furthermore, our results indicate that outflows are widespread throughout galaxy disks, often extending hundreds of kiloparsecs due to intense feedback from massive stars or active galactic nuclei. Despite their extensive reach, we observe that star formation persists within these outflow regions, suggesting that outflows do not always immediately suppress stellar activity, contrary to some expectations.

Using a multiphase transport (AMPT) model, we examine $v_3$ in central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}$ = 200 GeV. Pressure anisotropy generated by the geometry of initial conditions is identified as the primary driver for triangular flow ($v_3$), while that arising from initial energy density anisotropy plays a secondary role. Our findings indicate that the magnitude of $v_3$ scales linearly with the initial geometric anisotropy, yielding an enhancement factor of approximately 1.5 compared to $v_2$; by contrast, $v_3$ generated via dynamical anisotropy accounts for only about 0.1 times the total $v_2$. Furthermore, $v_3$ increases with higher collision energies, reaching a value of roughly 0.15 times $v_2$ in proton-proton interactions.

Open Knowledge Graphs (OGs) have grown substantially, enabling diverse applications; however, this expansion has resulted in significant data duplication and the adoption of inconsistent schemas. Datasets frequently integrate information from multiple sources, leading to accumulated errors that hinder the reliability of OGs and their associated services. Although data cleaning efforts aim to address these issues, the data often remains dispersed and difficult to reconcile. Furthermore, the information structure within OGs makes quality assurance inherently complex. To resolve these challenges, we introduce "CQL," a query-based framework designed to assess and evaluate data within open knowledge graphs. CQL facilitates the automatic derivation of data quality rules from queries and supports the identification of both explicit and implicit facts. By enabling the detection of anomalies such as data duplication, CQL empowers users to perform comprehensive assessments of open knowledge knowledge graphs.

Statistical inference methods for parametric models in discretely observed dynamic systems are notoriously difficult to develop. This paper introduces a new class of robust estimators designed to handle such estimations effectively. We demonstrate that these methods possess strong asymptotic properties and are validated through various simulation studies. Additionally, we apply the approach to estimate parameters in the AFT-Gamma duality model and compare results against traditional techniques using data from a clinical trial.

We present optical emission-line data for six Type 1 Seyfert galaxies, collected from the literature and supplemented with our own observations, to map their ionization cones. By calculating the [OIII]/[OII] ratio, we identified six instances where the ratio exceeds 3, indicating regions dominated by active galactic nucleus (AGN) ionization situated off the established ionization cone axis. In each case, this off-axis high-ratio area aligns with a prominent ionization-sensitive line, specifically either [OIII]$\lambda$5007 or [OIII]$\lambda$4959. Conversely, line-of-sight regions dominated by the host galaxy's stellar population show [OIII]/[OII] values below 1.5, with the [OII] line typically dominating the spectrum. Although the data points are limited, our findings suggest that the base of the ionization cone might be broader than the primary axis itself. Furthermore, the alignment of these outlier regions with specific [OIII] wavelengths offers preliminary support for the scenario proposed by Koss et al. (2017), suggesting the cone base could be defined by a bow shock formed where the ionization outflow intersects the circumnuclear disk.

Modern internet architectures are evolving to process a greater volume of data closer to the source, utilizing edge computing. This approach enables data collection and preliminary filtering at the network edge, with only the most critical information transmitted to the cloud. This concept is known as fog computing. To support these systems, the F0EVE framework has been developed as a functional-driven evaluation function. F0EVE allows edge applications to be defined declaratively, automatically generating the necessary code for deployment across fog and cloud infrastructures. This framework incorporates specialized functions for real-time data validation at the network boundary, ensuring only highly relevant and reliable insights reach the central cloud.
