Our work focuses on developing an automated method for generating synthetic traffic snapshots that mirror actual driving conditions. This capability is vital for advancing autonomous vehicle technology, as it enables robustness training by augmenting limited real-world data with diverse, complex, and rare traffic events. However, existing solutions often fall short because they either rely heavily on manual labor or produce images indistinguishable from hand-crafted diagrams rather than convincing realistic alternatives. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SceneGen, a novel framework that leverages deep generative adversarial networks (GANs) to produce traffic scenes grounded in the structural logic of schematic sketches yet visually seamless with photographic data. SceneGen operates through a two-stage pipeline: first, a high-fidelity encoder translates images into corresponding traffic schematics, capturing elements such as vehicles, lane markings, and road curbs; subsequently, a dedicated decoder utilizes these schematics as a generative prior to synthesize images rich in realistic textures and appearances. We evaluated SceneGen using the nuScenes dataset, where it was compared against collections of diverse and complex manual annotations. Beyond demonstrating a significant improvement in visual similarity to ground truth images, our approach also facilitates the creation of scenarios involving complex and rare traffic situations that are difficult to capture manually, while maintaining a cost far lower than extensive human effort.

Discretisations designed to preserve continuous properties, such as conservation laws or dissipation, have gained significant attention in the scientific community. While standard analysis indicates that standard second-order explicit time-stepping methods approximate these discrete properties with only first-order accuracy, novel numerical approaches have recently been developed to achieve full spectral accuracy for conserved and dissipated quantities. A typical characteristic of these high-order structure-preserving methods is their high order of linear stability, which often results in an excessively small stable time step when applied to stiff problems. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of preconditioned Krylov methods, specifically GMRES, as a solution to this time-step restriction issue. The analysis establishes a theoretical framework for assessing the accuracy of these discretised structures when applied to preconditioned systems, concluding that structure-preserving properties can be maintained to within $O(h^2)$ numerical residual errors. Numerical experiments are provided to validate these theoretical findings.

This work examines the evolution of interstellar dust particles in low-metallicity ($Z$) molecular clouds at low redshifts ($z$), specifically targeting $z \leq 1$, focusing on conditions around and within star-forming regions. The analysis evaluates dust growth timescales relative to the lifespans of associated low-mass stars and high-mass stars, considering three distinct low-$Z$ environments: (i) the solar neighborhood, (ii) the outskirts of young star clusters, and (iii) the crowded cores of these clusters. Dust dynamics were simulated using a one-dimensional Lagrangian framework that incorporates coagulation, accretion, shattering, and collisional vaporization. The study investigates dust opacity in regions near and within super-nova (SNe) explosions, modeling the interaction between SNe shocks and dust in various $Z$ settings. The results indicate that dust growth timescales are shorter in the dense, high-pressure zones near star clusters compared to the solar neighborhood. Furthermore, dust opacity is found to be reduced in the circum-SNe environments across all low-$Z$ scenarios. While the high energy of SNe shocks can destroy dust, significant net accumulation of dust is possible in these regions if the rate of dust destruction remains lower than the rate of production.

This work examines the challenges of Far-Field 3D Recognition (FF3DR), focusing on robust recognition of targets from a distance of 20 meters using only a single image. We introduce Far3Det, a framework designed to detect and identify objects in the far field from 3D models. The method begins by extracting a 3D model from the background of the image, followed by generating a virtual camera trajectory to synthesize a comprehensive set of 2D images from that model. Finally, an identifier is trained on this extensive dataset to detect and classify the 3D object in the image. We contribute a thorough background on FF3DR and provide a new large-scale dataset containing real-world far-field scenarios and corresponding 3D models for training and evaluation. We also supply a versatile FF3DR benchmark, which includes existing and newly proposed FF3DR detectors. Testing confirms that Framework-F and F-F detectors achieve an average precision of 17.6% on the dataset, marking a 10.8% improvement over the best previous method.

Finding ground states for quantum many-body systems is a core challenge in condensed matter physics, a domain where traditional numerical techniques often falter due to the sign problem encountered with finite-density Fermionic systems or infinite-precision requirements. To address this, we introduce a quantum machine learning framework designed to generate ground states by training on data from exact diagonalization. While the ground-state wavefunctions of non-trained isomorphic systems remain unknown to the method due to its lack of incorporation of specific physical symmetries or constraints, our tests reveal a remarkable capability: the generator produces highly accurate ground-state approximations for various compounds, including those not present in the initial training dataset.

Non-rigid volume-to-surface registration represents a significant challenge in medical imaging, particularly given the difficulty of acquiring 3D volumetric data in the clinic. To address this, we propose a novel method that generates a registration model using pairs of volumetric data and the corresponding surface markers applied during data collection. This approach involves formulating a mechanical framework that incorporates a data-driven constitutive law, where the material parameters are optimized through the alignment of a deformed organ surface to a target surface. The resulting model enables the registration of an organ surface to a target surface surface and the prediction of the associated volumetric data. Validated on the heart using a finite element-based mechanical solver, our experiments demonstrate that this method achieves high accuracy, is robust to noise, and maintains stability across variations in membrane thickness and material properties. Furthermore, the resulting deformable registration model allows for the retrospective analysis of clinical image sets, facilitating the alignment of 3D ultrasound scans to reference CT scans.

The paper investigates the infinitesimal conformal transformations preserving the energy-momentum tensor under the assumption of spherical symmetry and stationarity in spacetime. Through a detailed analysis of the associated system of partial differential equations, all possible, non-trivial spacetime-dependent forms of the tensor are identified. Furthermore, within this context, specific conformal vector fields are derived. The study reveals three distinct scenarios for the tensor's functional structure, each linked to a separate subclass of these vectors. Consequently, the necessary conditions required to generate valid, non-trivial tensors of this type are explicitly outlined.

Scene flow represents a fundamental 3D motion understanding capability for humans and robots alike, enabling the interpretation of complex movements. Although deep learning has significantly enhanced the precision of flow prediction, it typically relies on massive datasets for training. A key breakthrough in this domain is the introduction of self-supervised training methods, which leverage the inherent geometry of data to learn representations without explicit labels. In this paper, we introduce a novel adversarial metric learning approach designed to extend self-supervised learning capabilities to even broader scenarios. We evaluate our method specifically on challenging flow estimation tasks, demonstrating that learned adversarial metrics can successfully discriminate positive data samples from corrupted variants in a problem-agnostic manner. Furthermore, we show that training a scene flow estimator using this learned metric achieves performance nearly identical to that of traditional supervised training. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/raffaelli/Adversarial-Metric-Learning.

We introduce a low-power, high-precision classification approach grounded in the approximation of polynomial forms by rational functions. In this framework, a polynomial classifier is transformed into a Spiking Random Neural Network (SRNN) that evaluates the rational function $R(x)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}a_{i}x^{k_{i}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{K}b_{i}x^{k_{i}}}$. We demonstrate that training this network is unnecessary; instead, optimal parameters are derived analytically from the trained equivalent polynomial neural classifier. We provide a detailed description of the SRNN design, including its theoretical underpinnings, implementation specifics, and performance metrics. Experimental results indicate that this method achieves a 100-fold reduction in power consumption and a 1.5-fold improvement in precision when processing 28x28 grayscale images compared to traditional artificial neural networks utilizing artificial memristors. Furthermore, when applied to 122-dimensional speech recognition data, the system matches the accuracy of standard artificial neural networks while utilizing artificial memristors, all within a hardware footprint of a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) dedicated to speech classification.

We specifically analyze how this field influences equation of state and other thermodynamic metrics in such systems. Results are visualized through various plots illustrating the equation of state and key thermodynamic quantities across different temperatures and external magnetic field intensities.

Modern microservices architectures rely heavily on containerization, making system call (syscall) filtering a critical security measure. However, traditional filtering methods often hinder the performance of these lightweight containers. To address this, we present **Timeloop**, a system that employs syscalls as inputs for **Large Language Model (LLM)**-driven policy generation, automatically determining the most effective filtering strategies to optimize both the security and performance of microservices running in containers.

We examine the stability of dark matter (DM) within the framework of the $B-L$ extension of the Standard Model, augmenting the model with three right-handed neutrinos and two complex scalar singlets. This results in four potential DM candidates: two pseudo-Goldstone bosons and two scalar fields, all of which must satisfy stringent DM proton-disappearance constraints from the SBN experiment at Fermilab. Specifically, the singlet scalars rely on specific couplings to evade detection, whereas the pseudo-Goldstone bosons inherently avoid the proton-disappearance channel due to $B-L$ symmetry, rendering them robust against such experimental limits. Furthermore, by incorporating decay mechanisms for both the $\Delta$ and \delta$ fields into $X$-ray spectra, we demonstrate that consistent regions exist where these components contribute to DM in this theoretical structure.

This work addresses the Bayesian multi-object density estimation challenge under an independent birth-and-death dynamic, incorporating components for false alarms, undetected objects, and independent targets. The proposed Persistent Multi-Blade (PMBM) filter structures multi-object density by decoupling it into separate track density (representing likely tracks with uncertain attributes) and isolated single-object densities, thereby enabling more streamlined recursion. Within the filter's framework, a hybrid grid-free/guided approach is developed for the origin likelihood function. This method assigns grid points based on object age thresholds to approximate density: these points feed a guided hypothesis using a PPMF (generalized multi-1) distribution for tracks, while grid-free functions are applied to single-object density. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this method achieves a low computational burden with performance nearly matching the full grid-free system. Additionally, the paper utilizes this efficient algorithm to optimize the myopic sensor assignment problem, specifically optimizing one grid point per potential sensor to maximize the trace of the generalized multi-1 covariance matrix.

This study introduces a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach designed to improve soccer decisions during pivotal game moments. Initially, we formalize the match situation as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and suggest a corresponding reward function optimized through multi-objective learning. To manage decision-making within various in-game contexts, we established distinct DRL agents, each specialized for a specific game state. Empirical results indicate that incorporating DRL decision support into professional matches—specifically those of the UEFA Champions League—yields more favorable outcomes compared to historic performance, demonstrating the method's potential to elevate on-field choices.

Extended sources, such as the ocean surface or weather fronts, emit signals that provide critical insights into their physical characteristics and dynamic behaviors. Although current research focuses on point-source inversion techniques, there is a lack of methodologies dedicated to extending these approaches for infinite radiation sources. This paper introduces a framework for time-domain inversion of acoustic sources that assume infinite lateral extent. We demonstrate analytically that the time-domain transfer function linking an extended source to a receiver can be derived directly from the point-source Green's function. Leveraging this relationship, we develop an efficient computational strategy to generate synthetic pressure fields from extended sources, achieving performance comparable to the analytical solution while circumventing the prohibitive costs of standard numerical propagation techniques. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical equivalence between time-domain extended source propagation and a specific class of two-dimensional time-domain problems. Using this foundation, we formulate a novel finite difference time domain (FDTD) scheme designed to simulate the time-domain response of an acoustic field to extended source emission. Finally, we validate our methodology through numerical experiments conducted in both synthetic environments and full-scale oceanic settings.

Although the optical asymmetry parameter helps characterize chiral media, its application in linear optics has historically been limited due to the difficulty in independently adjusting asymmetry and chirality. We propose that utilizing the amplitude-squeezed vacuum field incident on a lossy $\chi^{(2)}$ nonlinear medium serves as an effective solution for achieving directional parametric fluorescence. Our findings demonstrate that by varying the degree of quantum squeezing applied to the vacuum field, one can not only match the level of optical asymmetry found in standard chi-plus-one reflection from fully chiral media but also surpass it, reaching a maximum asymmetry factor of 12. Furthermore, the intrinsic sensitivity of this effect to material losses presents a novel avenue for sensing chiral and asymmetric coupling losses through the measurement of the optical asymmetry parameter within the medium.

This study utilizes data from the AstroSat mission to examine X-ray observations of the X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst. The satellite's Cadance instrument detected a broad spectral energy peak at approximately 30 keV, while the lags measured by Time-Correlated Single-Photon (TCSP) revealed a noise hump at roughly 10 Hz. Analysis of the Cadance time-series data identified a quasi-periodic oscillation (QPO) with a central frequency of 1.98 ± 0.01 Hz, which persisted for roughly 10 kiloseconds throughout the observation. The QPO frequency displayed a positive correlation with the X-ray flux, shifting from 1.98 ± 0.01 Hz at 1.58 counts s$^{-1}$ to 2.02 ± 0.01 Hz at 2.13 counts s$^{-1}$; this behavior is indicative of the positive frequency-flux shift typically associated with the accretion disk. Furthermore, the scanning Spectro-Codage (SC) instrument recorded a cyclotron emission line centered at 25.7 ± 0.4 keV. Based on these cyclotron line parameters, the magnetic field strength at the neutron star's surface is calculated to be approximately 5.1 × 10$^{12}$ G.

This study examines a spatially explicit elector model incorporating competition-colonization tradeoffs to analyze noise-induced species exclusion and coexistence. In this framework, the species with a competitive edge lacks the ability to displace others, while the inferior competitor possesses colonization advantages. Mathematical analysis via a stochastic lattice gas elector approach yields three distinct outcomes: (i) dominance by the superior species, (ii) coexistence through competitive displacement, and (iii) coexistence via segregation. Furthermore, the study focuses on a scenario where species interact exclusively within their own domains, resulting in coexistence via domain formation. Findings indicate that noise-induced domain creation favors the species with higher dispersal rates, whereas noise-induced segregation allows dominance by the competitive leader.

Sundials, which utilize the sun's position to indicate the time, constitute one of humanity's earliest timekeeping inventions. While often associated with Western traditions, these instruments are also prevalent in Indonesia, known locally as *suryakala-nusantara*. Derived from Javanese words for "sun" and "correctly measure," *suryakala-nusantara* was historically employed in royal courts to orchestrate daily schedules, including prayers, meals, and official duties. Although their symbolic importance in reconstructing old temporal systems is acknowledged, the lack of documentation regarding their operational principles and the absence of functional replicas have hindered their study. Addressing this, the present research employs the examination of an 18th-century specimen from the Javanese Sultanate to analyze the device's mechanism and intended purpose. The study posits that *suryakala-nusantara* functions as a true sundial by demonstrating, through shadow analysis and computational modeling, that its time readings align with astronomical expectations. Furthermore, the research reveals that the intricate carvings adorning the instrument serve a practical purpose: they facilitate time determination without necessitating disassembly of the device.

This paper introduces an Integrated Data and Energy Networking (DEN) model designed to support bidirectional device-to-device (D2D) communications within Integrated Data and Energy Networking (DEN) model, where D2D links transmit information via direct wireless transmission, while simultaneously harvesting energy from the information signals of other D2D pairs. The core of the proposed solution is a suboptimal, low-complexity subchannel allocation algorithm grounded in the concept of cognitive reflection surfaces (CRSs). This algorithm determines the optimal reflectivity coefficients for the CRSs to maximize the aggregate energy harvested by D2D links, subject to constraints on data transmission rates. Subsequently, the algorithm assigns subchannels to D2D pairs based on the derived reflectivity coefficients to ensure that data transmission rates for all pairs meet the minimum required thresholds. Numerical evaluations confirm that the CRSs significantly enhance the total energy harvested by D2D links, and the resulting bit-energy trade-off demonstrates the algorithm's superior performance.

This study details the remote deployment of a single-component LDV setup to generate two-dimensional velocity datasets. By utilizing only one LDV beam, the measurement plane was defined through the intersection of the light sheet's plane with the natural flow layer, eliminating the need for sheet alignment against a physical wall surface. Validation of this approach was conducted in a turbulent boundary layer at a unit Reynolds number of $5 \times 10^6 m/s$ on the suction side of an airfoil, 0.005 chord lengths ($c$) away from the trailing edge. Velocity data were collected across 0.0025 $c$ intervals starting from 0.005 $c$ and extending to 0.02 $c$ in the streamwise direction. The resulting velocity profiles, when compared against existing literature, demonstrated strong agreement, thereby confirming the accuracy of the distant measurement technique.

Although variations in sample and microscope conditions often introduce unwanted phase and amplitude distortations, currently available phase plates in the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) lack the ability to correct these imperfections. This study evaluates whether a TEM-compatible programmable phase plate can be utilized to correct specific higher-order distortations. By simulating the imaging of gold nanoparticles under both ideal and distorted electron potentials, we assess the efficacy of this plate in representing higher-order phase and amplitude correctors. Results indicate that while a 180-degree phase plate configuration is optimal for enhancing image contrast in distorted potentials, a 90-degree setting more accurately reconstructs the true potential of the particle. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a 180-degree plate can effectively eliminate a specific third-order (3,0) distortion, serving as a corrector for that particular higher-order anomaly.

In recent years, significant advancements in conversational AI have been driven by improved language understanding capabilities. Consequently, most current research prioritizes enhancing the quality of input representations. In this work, we challenge the prevailing assumption that these state-of-the-art models require constant updates to their encoders for improved task performance. Instead, we propose that the information necessary to support specific tasks is already embedded within the representations generated by the model itself. To validate this hypothesis, we conducted a comprehensive investigation into the features of inputs from two prominent models—Open Dialogue (OD) and Chatbot Arena (CA)—across a diverse range of in-domain and cross-domain dialogues. Our analysis, which included both qualitative and quantitative assessments, yielded three primary findings: first, a distinct separation exists between the encodings of task-relevant and irrelevant inputs; second, these patterns hold true for both OD and CA, remain consistent across different tasks, and are largely independent of the source domain of the data; and third, these distinctions are more pronounced for CA compared to OD.

Ground LiDAR-based place recognition is essential for global localization and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) in robotics. Given its significance, numerous feature extraction methods have been developed, ranging from hand-crafted techniques to advanced deep learning approaches. Although existing deep learning methods effectively achieve high recognition accuracy, they frequently demand extensive feature dimensions and significant computational resources, particularly when processing unaligned 3D LiDLiD scans. To address this, we introduce an attention-based deep learning framework, termed "AttDLNet," designed for recognizing place from 3D LiDAR data. This framework incorporates two key components: a 3D voxel convolutional network enhanced with an attention mechanism for feature learning, and a refined nearest neighbor search algorithm. The attention mechanism dynamically prioritizes critical and distinctive feature voxels, enabling the system to deliver accurate recognition while utilizing reduced-dimensional features. At high-energy colliders, the stringent constraints on the properties of light dark matter are largely dictated by the sensitivity of missing energy searches, which in turn depend on the dark sector's ability to produce highly boosted, long-lived particles that evade current detector capabilities. This study investigates an alternative avenue for these limitations by examining the decay of neutral mesons into particles with dark sector degrees of freedom. Specifically, we examine the decay $B^0 \to B_s^0 + a$, where $a$ denotes a single axial-vector dark photon. We find that Belle II and SuperKEKB can constrain the CP-even production of $a$ for masses between 1.5 and 4.5 GeV/c$^2, with the sensitivity range shifting based on the specific kinematics of the dark sector.

We investigated how well contextualized language models perform in identifying semantic change detection, a task that involves recognizing words with the same dictionary definition but differing contextual implications. The spins of heavy quasars are significantly influenced by the formation of boson clouds surrounding rotating black holes through the mechanism of superradiance, a process that is particularly effective for ultralight bosons with masses below $10^{-10}$ eV. This study investigates the superspin evolution of three specific quasar hosts—M33-EB3, MAXI 0046+00, and XTE J1559-302—and identifies characteristic signatures in their spin parameters that constrain ultralight scalar and axion candidates. Neuronal migration is a fundamental aspect of brain development, and retinogenesis serves as a key model for studying this phenomenon. In both embryonic and adult retinas, neurons traverse distinct vertical positions within the neural tissue without changing their overall orientation, a behavior termed "interkinetic nuclear movement" (IKNM). This study proposes a novel theoretical framework that integrates biological constraints with statistical physics to investigate the diffusion-driven mechanics of IKNM in developing retinas. Observations reveal that in young embryos, nuclei follow a cyclical pattern of diffusion, shifting from the inner to the outer boundary and back, whereas in more mature embryos, this movement becomes unidirectional as diffusion proceeds from the outer layers inwardly. We note a direct correlation between the timing of IKNM and the regulation of the zebrafish mitotic cycle. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the specific displacement of these nuclei is governed by an active transport mechanism, which functions in opposition to the cytoskeletal forces of the surrounding extracellular matrix.

Source separation serves as a cornerstone technique in video processing, enabling individual layer extraction from videos composed as linear superpositions. Consequently, it has been successfully applied to video compressive sensing and color video demosaicing. In this study, source separation is framed within natural video coding, where the goal is to recover video data using codes designed to model natural video characteristics. The research introduces a novel class of codes termed "separable codes," which facilitate the isolation of source layers such as luminance, chrominance, and depth maps. These codes integrate separable convolutional filters with sparse coding, where the codebooks for both factor matrices and sparse coefficients are derived from their respective training sets. The proposed code structure is then incorporated into video source separation systems, which are trained via an end-to-end strategy. The resulting system is evaluated on a synthetic dataset generated from combined layers and a real dataset of compressed-sensing videos. The study confirms that this approach yields state-of-the-art performance, delivering superior quality in both chroma demosaicing and compressive sensing video reconstruction.

This study examines incompressible polar active liquids containing quelled self-propelled particles that consume energy to move, contrasting them with non-conserving motile types. Within the hydrodynamic framework, we derive a non-linear diffusion equation governing the hydrological transition from a disordered state to one of polarity. We establish that quelled polar active matter cannot sustain a fluid of self-driven constituents, a fundamental distinction from its motile counterpart. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for non-conserving particles, increasing either propulsion speed or density inevitably triggers a transition into an ordered state. Conversely, for quelled particles, both speed and density have opposing or negligible impacts on ordering; specifically, increasing density actually hinders the transition to order, while the critical speed required for ordering diminishes as density increases. These theoretical predictions can be validated through experiments utilizing quelled bacteria such as *Chlamydomonas*.

At any given moment, a deterministic dynamical system possesses a unique state, yet it can possess multiple distinct long-term behaviors known as coexisting attractors. Identifying these alternative outcomes is crucial for accurately modeling and forecasting real-world phenomena, such as the oscillations observed in cardiac tissue. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a streamlined approach that efficiently locates coexisting attractors by leveraging the properties of H\'enon maps. This strategy was validated on a physiological model of cardiac contraction and expansion, successfully revealing a previously unobserved oscillatory state.

Data augmentation serves as a critical technique for enhancing generalization in deep learning, yet generating diverse and varied data remains difficult, particularly for data-inhibited models. Existing solutions often rely on data-centric approaches that demand large volumes of training samples to produce sufficient diversity, or on black-box generative models that require continuous tuning of their generators. In this paper, we introduce a novel generative model designed to create diverse, periodic functional images using minimal data. Our approach formulates diversity through structured periodic activations modulated by sinusoidal signals. This framework enables the efficient training of a generalizable encoder-decoder architecture capable of generating diverse outputs. We demonstrate the model's effectiveness across multiple benchmarks using both real- and synthetic-generated data.

The semantic categorization of natural stimuli by humans and other animals largely depends on distinguishing living from non-living entities. While prior research suggests this differentiation exists across various levels of the visual processing hierarchy, it remains unclear whether the segregation of animacy specifically occurs within the ventral temporal cortex (VTC), a brain region crucial for object recognition and semantic processing. Using neuroimaging data from healthy participants, we analyzed fMRI responses to a comprehensive stimulus set encompassing animals, humans, and diverse inanimate objects. Our findings reveal that neuroimaging data robustly differentiate how the brain processes animacy in these visual and auditory areas, with statistical power remaining strong even when controlling for low-level visual attributes and fine-grained motion cues. Furthermore, when neuroimaging data were combined with the features of stimulus images, animacy classification achieved near-perfect accuracy; notably, minimal dimensional reductions in these features still sustained high predictive performance. However, when tested against a variety of other semantic dimensions using both extensive stimulus features and highly reduced dimensional representations, animacy consistently yielded the most accurate predictions. These results substantiate that organizing stimuli by animates is a fundamental component of the hierarchical semantic structure of the brain's recognition systems.

In relational program verification, traditional logical pre- and postconditions are replaced by invariant relations maintained across related programs. Furthermore, we introduce a practical rule set suitable for real-world programs and prove its soundness and completeness with respect to a efficiently computable, orthogonal complexity measure.

Super-spreader incidents, a hallmark of epidemics, receive substantial attention yet remain difficult to study due to their stochastic nature and rarity. This paper introduces a novel mathematical framework designed to model these events within the broader context of the SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) model, which tracks population transitions through infection and recovery. Within this approach, individuals move from susceptibility to infection in two ways: through standard pairwise contacts governed by the model's transmission rate, or via unpredictable super-spreader occurrences affecting multiple hosts at once. We analytically derive the model's basic reproduction number ($R_0$) and the final major outbreak size, characterizing the stochastic element via a probability distribution of spreaders. Neural networks have recently been employed to infer vector solar magnetic fields from linear polarization observations, offering a significant leap in both spatial resolution and temporal frequency. Nevertheless, this research examines whether such inferred datasets harbor biases that could affect subsequent scientific analyses. This study introduces a novel methodology for bias detection, applying it to evaluate the performance of two prominent algorithms: St. Petersburg's DeepSF and Washington's Wavelet Transform Neural Network (WTNN). The application of these techniques to observations from the National Solar Observatory's Dunn Solar Telescope yielded inferred magnetic field estimates that demonstrated superior fidelity compared to VSMAP vector magnetogram benchmarks. Despite this overall agreement, a distinct negative correlation bias was identified in the data produced by DeepSF and WTNN relative to the VSMAP reference. This bias likely stems from the training data used for these models, which incorporated negative correlations between certain Stokes parameters present in the VSMAP magnetograms. Although the study notes that raw WTNN output data exhibited an additional bias in the width of magnetic flux structures, a new uniform preprocessing step for training and/or inference data is proposed to mitigate these artifacts. Ultimately, the paper emphasizes the necessity of developing robust strategies to recognize and eliminate such biases to ensure the full utility of upcoming high-cadence, high-resolution solar magnetic field records.

The stellar dynamics of young stellar clusters (YSCs) serve as a primary mechanism for galaxy evolution, largely determined by their interaction with host galactic environments, which can lead to either early disruption or the development of globular clusters through core collapse. A critical factor in these processes is the radius of YSCs; our study utilizes data from the Legacy Survey for Local Area Galaxy YSCs catalog to investigate radius distributions across seven nearby galaxies, including the Milky Way. We find that the cumulative radius distribution follows a power law with a slope of $1.75 \pm 0.04$, consistent with results from other research. Additionally, our analysis reveals Hubble-fringe effects, where YSCs in galaxies like M31 and NGC 253 exhibit larger radii than those in central regions, a pattern supported by literature. Most notably, we observe a new trend where the median radii of YSCs in NGC 4303 and NGC 253 show a decline as distance from the galaxy's center increases. This counterintuitive result contrasts with the standard paradigm, which predicts environmental processes would restrict clusters in dense central regions more severely. We suggest that the infall of gas and subsequent gravitational potential changes in the central regions of NGC 4303 and NGC 253 may explain this phenomenon, highlighting the necessity for further investigation into the central dynamics of nearby galaxies to clarify YSC evolution.

Utilizing the Wallenzsteinberger-ackoff (WF) formalism, we have developed a innovative lattice QCD approach to determine the decay width for $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$. This strategy involves gauging two photons couple to the $\eta_c$ via a heavy quark vector meson, which allows the process to occur within a single lattice configuration. Consequently, this technique demands significantly fewer statistics than previous approaches that calculate the photon field strength tensor directly. We performed our computations on an $8^3 \times 4$ lattice employing an ensemble of quenched gauge configurations to evaluate the necessary correlation functions. Using these results, we extracted the $\eta_c \rightarrow 2\gamma$ decay rate, yielding a value of $5.4(10) \times 10^{-3} GeV$ using the lattice determination of the $\eta_c$ mass ($M_{\eta_c} = 2983(10) MeV$). This result aligns well with experimental data and other recent lattice QCD findings.

This work introduces the concept of fragile integers, defined by the property that dividing them by any prime factor $p$ results in an integer $q$ which possesses at least as many prime factors (counted with multiplicity) as $q$ has total digits in the decimal system. This paper introduces a new algorithm known as M-ar-K-Fast (M-ar-K-Fast), designed to enhance the M-ar-K (M-ar-K) algorithm. Additionally, the study evaluates performance across varying input types, including real, complex, positive, negative, and mixed numerical values. Results indicate that the M-ar-K-Fast algorithm achieves a performance boost of approximately 1.5 times faster than the existing 2D-FFT algorithm.

Establishing optimal hyperparameters for deep learning models through traditional grid or random search is often prohibitively costly when implementing strong differential privacy (DP), necessitating the use of suboptimal parameters for DP-SGD training. Furthermore, the addition of noise introduces a complex, non-linear landscape for hyperparameter interactions, causing standard methods to fail in finding effective private solutions. This approach treats both the selection algorithm and the DP-SGD training process as back-to-back private mechanisms sharing a combined privacy budget, ensuring that the combined impact remains acceptable. Through extensive experiments with various private neural networks, we demonstrate that our method surpasses existing random private searches by up to 200\%, resulting in significantly improved model accuracy.

The Euclid mission, a cornerstone of the ESA Cosmic Vision 2015–2025 program, is designed to investigate the nature of dark energy and the formation of structures through observations of weak gravitational lensing and the measurement of the arclet catalog spectrum (WGS). A primary instrument for this endeavor is the Near-Infrared and Optical Imaging Spectrograph (NISP), which will operate on the Euclid spacecraft. This study examines the impact of correlated noise on flux measurements in the context of Euclid's NISP instrument. We find that the noise is likely to have a significant impact on the accuracy of flux measurements, potentially leading to systematic biases in the final arclet catalog spectrum. We also find that the impact of correlated noise is likely to be more pronounced for sources with lower signal-to-noise ratios. Finally, we note that the effect of correlated noise may be mitigated by using multiple exposures.

We introduce a two-method statistical framework designed to investigate the link between stellar characteristics and their derived physical properties. Employing the methodological diversity inherent in stellar spectroscopy, this model utilizes a combination of machine learning techniques and maximum likelihood estimation. By leveraging the extensive dataset of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's Data Release 16 (APOGEE), we demonstrate that this dual-approach strategy outperforms single-method implementations. Specifically, when applied to elemental abundance analyses, the model achieves a 10% improvement in classification metrics and reduces total systematic errors by 30%. Such an enhancement in precision and accuracy is vital for the precise characterization of stellar populations and the mapping of the interstellar medium. Using this refined model on disk stellar data, we examine the correlations between metallicity and other chemical elements, as well as the relationships among various elements. Our findings reveal that the age-related trends observed in the data are an artifact of the specific model employed. Furthermore, the study identifies three distinct chemical substructures within the galactic disk, which may signify different modes of star formation activity.

Beginning in December 2019, the novel coronavirus disease (COVID-19) emerged in China, prompting widespread public anxiety and a surge in false information disseminated via social media. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 199,902 tweets related to COVID-19 collected from Weibo between December 2019 and February 22, 2020, this study identifies the primary clusters of online rumors, maps their transmission mechanisms, and assesses the spreading influence of the most prominent rumor accounts. The findings indicate that these tweets reached a total of 159.6 million users, with 21,591 tweets classified as rumor content originating from 1,114 distinct accounts. The research further reveals a "two-tier" structure among rumor-spreading accounts, characterized by 100 high-influence nodes responsible for 90% of the rumor propagation, while 1,014 low-influence nodes accounted for only 10% of the spread. Additionally, the study analyzes the growth trajectories of these accounts and their respective audiences. Ultimately, this paper offers novel theoretical insights and data-driven methodologies for analyzing and measuring online rumors, providing significant implications for enhancing public health interventions and improving future anti-epidemic strategies.

The loss function is fundamental to a deep neural network's architecture, governing the optimization of network weights by guiding the training process. Consequently, selecting an appropriate loss function is critical for ensuring a model achieves high performance on its intended task. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of various loss functions within deep neural networks used for image classification. We analyze the implications of these function choices by examining classification accuracy, study convergence rates, and measuring sensitivity to the learning rate. Furthermore, we explore how differing component structures within specific loss functions influence overall model behavior. To validate these findings, we conducted experiments using ResNet-50 for image classification across three distinct datasets: ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and SVHN.

This study establishes the $L^2$-stability of Navier-Stokes equations for sufficiently high spatial dimensions under slimited backflow controllers defined on oblique portions of the domain boundary. These findings hold for both externally forced and invadience scenarios, demonstrating global stabilities for all initial data within the critical $L^2$-space setting. Additionally, we prove the global attractionor property of steady solutions, with exponential rates of convergence guaranteed for restricted initial conditions. A pivotal finding supporting these results is the novel, space-independent $L^3$-dissipation estimate applicable to these slanted setups, which resolves an issue previously unresolved in the literature.

This study introduces a novel numerical simulation technique for integrated thermomechanical analysis, specifically designed to model strain-induced crystallization (SIC) in polymer composites filled with liquid crystal (LC) nanoparticles. The proposed approach employs a newly developed constitutive framework that accounts for the thermomechanical coupling between the polymer matrix and the SIC process of LC particles. By integrating a thermal network approach with a heat balance equation, the simulation addresses the intricate heat exchange mechanisms between the SIC occurring within LC particles and the surrounding polymer matrix, thereby enabling the calculation of heat generation and exchange. Validation of the simulation was achieved through comparative analysis with experimental data, demonstrating its capability to accurately predict the microstructural development of composites under both isothermal and adiabatic conditions. Furthermore, the model successfully captures experimentally observed phenomena, including the acceleration of SIC and the formation of flow-aligned textures resulting from viscous heat generation during deformation. These findings collectively substantiate the reliability of the proposed constitutive model and associated heat transfer methodology, offering a robust foundation for predictive simulations of microstructure evolution in SIC-based polymer composites.

This study examines the effects of Pauli magnetism on magnetically ordered phases within a superconductor exhibiting nematicity, specifically focusing on d$_{x^2-y^2}$-symmetric triplet pairing induced by p-wave spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and magnetic exchange interactions. In the absence of an external magnetic field, spontaneous magnetism arises solely from exchange forces. However, when applied, a critical field strength is required to induce full magnetic ordering; below this threshold exists a spin canting regime. Notably, the nematic cantination regime persists even after accounting for van Vleck susceptibility, which moderates exchange coupling strength. Furthermore, nematic cantination regimes show sensitivity to nematic orientation relative to both the momentum direction of Cooper pairs and the SOC vector. External magnetic fields exceeding the critical value can trigger transitions between collinear and orthogonal ordering states by manipulating the balance between exchange and spin-orbit interactions. Additionally, van Vleck susceptibility facilitates singlet pairing of degenerate spin components via isotropic Zeeman splitting, potentially stabilizing triplet magnetism against field-induced collapse toward singlet components.

The core challenge in learning control involves learning algorithms that interact with a dynamic environment. A primary obstacle is the lack of direct supervision, as most feedback is indirect and only available after a costly physical interaction. To address this, the paper proposes a framework for meta-learning rectifying feedback, enabling the rapid adaptation to new tasks using a feedback signal indicating whether performance was worse than a hidden benchmark. This method assumes feedback signals are sparse, yet enables fast learning by providing a clear learning target. The authors introduce a feedback-guided reduction that transforms any black-box stochastic convex optimization method into one capable of efficiently learning from such rectifying feedback. Results demonstrate that when combined with an efficient reduction, it achieves a sample complexity of $O(\log(1/\delta)\log(U/C)\log(R)\log(1/\epsilon))$, where $U$ and $C$ represent the ranges of feedback and advice, $R$ is the feedback latency, and $\delta$ and $\epsilon$ are the probabilities of failure and excess cost, respectively. The proposed feedback-guided reduction is then utilized to explore two scenarios: learning arm manipulation with feedback signals that allow a 3-log improvement in dependence on feedback latency $R$, and learning a quadruped robot to walk with feedback signals that allow a 3-log improvement in dependence on feedback latency $R$ and advice noise.

Circularly polarized modulation (CPM) is recognized for its low spectral density, robust resilience to linear channel impairments, and ease of implementation. Conventional non-coherent differential detection specifically targets CPM signals possessing a prescribed spectral shaping factor $h$ of $1/(2k)$, where $k$ is a positive integer. This non-coherent approach significantly simplifies the receiver architecture by eliminating the need for reference signal generation and synchronization, thereby reducing operational costs. However, such differential detection inherently involves a time delay equal to $2k$ symbol periods, which constrains applications requiring minimal latency. This study introduces an enhanced non-coherent differential detection method that retains these advantages while minimizing the delay to just $1/h \div 2k$ symbol times. Furthermore, numerical simulations confirm that this proposed technique maintains near-identical bit error rate (BER) performance compared to conventional schemes.

Black hole neutron star mergers (BH-NS) serve as crucial sources for multi-messenger astronomy, primarily because the surface disruption of the neutron star releases significant gravitational wave energy and often triggers a merger-induced supernova of the star's outer layers. The likelihood of detecting these events via gravitational waves and gamma-ray bursts hinges on the specific characteristics of the core-collapse dynamics, the presence of long-lived accretion-powered afterglows, and the timing of the event relative to the sensitive volume of third-generation detectors. This study examines various scenarios of core-collapse behavior in these systems, focusing on how they affect gamma-ray burst production, constraints on the neutron star equation of state, and the associated kilonova signals. We specifically analyze the roles of core collapse, successful or failed supernovae, and the generation of long-lived accretion disks. Additionally, we evaluate the impact of the sensitivity of future detectors, such as the Einstein Telescope, on observability. Our analysis indicates that even when core collapse halts the formation of a gamma-ray burst, the subsequent core bounce can still generate a distinctive signature in the gravitational wave signal.

A thermal state is defined as a mixed state that remains invariant under unitary transformations for any subset of its degrees of freedom. This paper investigates the thermal states of quantum fields, determining their entanglement entropy, entanglement spectrum, quantum capacity, and vacuum compressibility when applied to the Minkowski state and black hole states. It demonstrates that the low-energy dynamics of quantum fields thermatize into a universal effective model, identified as a universal maximally entangled state. Consequently, the coherence of quantum fields at low energies near a black hole or any Unruh-deWitt thermalization scenario is notably diminished. The findings indicate that the non-local correlations accessible within a low-energy effective model, described by $n$ degrees of freedom, can be accurately represented by a simple maximally entangled pair where each component involves only two degrees per system.

Rain generation and clearing represent inverse yet interconnected challenges, and addressing them jointly offers a pathway to more robust models. To this end, we introduce a new framework for the unified task of rain synthesis and removal. Our approach treats these processes as two phases of a closed loop, where the output of one phase serves as the input for the other, with the second phase tasked with recovering the original scene from the results produced by the first. We propose a new architecture, the Loop-based Joint Rain Removal and Generation (LoopNet), which employs two advanced yet interconnected generative models, the Realistic Precipitation Generation (RPG) and the Scene De-Raining (SDR) models. The loop is established through the integration of the output of the first model into the input of the second. This design enables the second model to learn how to purify precipitation-altered images, thereby enhancing its performance on real-world wet data. Conversely, the input provided by the second model allows the first to learn the specific characteristics of rain, improving overall generation quality. To facilitate this, we introduce a new disentanglement loss, the Loop-based Disentanglement (LDE) loss, which ensures that the rainfall removal model focuses solely on eliminating water while the generation model concentrates on recreating it. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on two major benchmarks for both rain generation and removal. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan1999/RainLoopNet.

A significant hurdle in reward learning remains the high cost associated with human annotations, especially for generating precise numerical rewards. Although current methods allow for efficient single-annotation per trajectory, the total number of required trajectories typically grows exponentially as the number of states increases. This study introduces a method that capitalizes on multi-label preference learning to substantially lower both the number of generations and the overall time spent on annotation. The proposed technique utilizes visual aggregation to construct compact reward clusters and employs an aided double-randomized sorting protocol to learn the underlying reward function. Efficacy has been validated across both simulated benchmarks and a practical robotics navigation task.

The Continuum hypothesis, introduced by Cantor, remains unresolved in standard set theory, as the size of the continuum can vary. This variability arises because one can assume the existence of cardinals with various properties relative to the continuum. Historically, researchers focused primarily on constructing specific models demonstrating these possibilities. In contrast, this paper investigates the Continuum problem through the lens of constructive model theory, utilizing tools such as consistency strength and model partnerships. We posit that the most natural mathematical setting for determining the size of the continuum involves adding just a single cardinal of sufficient strength. Furthermore, we propose that exploring other potential solutions to the Continuum problem benefits greatly from adopting a more theoretically robust framework.

This study examined how the Five Factor Model of personality relates to the likelihood of problematic substance use. Data was gathered from 1,000 participants aged 18 to 65, who completed measures assessing their Big Five traits, general drug use tendencies, and specific patterns of problematic consumption. Correlation and regression analyses revealed that all five personality domains show a significant link to adverse drug use behaviors. Notably, neuroticism and low conscientiousness were the primary drivers, together accounting for approximately 47% of the variance in these outcomes. These findings offer valuable insights for future research and practical applications in the field of addiction.

An emerging capability of large language models (LLMs), as suggested by recent studies, is their ability to master diverse tasks through the application of programmatically crafted if-then rules, often called synthetic or atomic reasoning. This work introduces ATOMIC, a comprehensive repository containing 11.5 million distinct simple reasoning rules and 90 million associated examples spanning 31 different domains. ATOMIC serves a dual function: it provides an extensive source of data for generating targeted RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) benchmarks and offers vast resources for foundational research in small model pre-training. Empirical results indicate that current LLMs, even when given domain-specific training data, frequently fail on ATOMIC's Retrieval-based tests. Furthermore, utilizing ATOMIC's high-quality synthetic data for training significantly improves model performance on the platform, surpassing other standard RAG configurations.

Although numerous applications for quantum computing remain distant, the capabilities of current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices are well-suited to support corporate strategies. This paper demonstrates the practical utility of NISQ devices in optimizing investment portfolios, utilizing an Enterprise-grade IBM quantum processor to execute an HHL algorithm iteration applicable to real-world portfolio improvements. By leveraging the limited quantum volume of NISQ hardware to perform a single HHL iteration, a full HHL run, or a hybrid approach combining a partial HHL execution with a classical least squares solver, this method effectively leverages limited device capabilities. The results indicate that such strategies can utilize a 50-qubit NISQ device to solve a covariance matrix involving 4444 asset variables, achieving a relative reduction in portfolio variance of 11.4% compared to a purely classical optimization.

We present experimental data from normal-state NbN nanowires, 5 nm in thickness and 1 $\mu$m in length, showing that quantum electrodynamics can be harnessed to influence the electrical conductivity of a superconductor. In these NbN quantum interference devices (QPIDs), we observe coherent quantum phase slips (QPS) resulting in a transition from a zero-resistance state to a steady current flow when a bias voltage is applied. Furthermore, the application of a gate-induced electrostatic field allows modulation of both the critical voltage required for a current switch-on and the voltage drop across the wire during the steady state. We demonstrate that these phenomena align with a model based on a single quantum phase slip, whereas a model relying solely on a single Josephson junction fails to account for the observed results.

Using the open-source spectral line retrieval code APOLLO, we conducted a comprehensive re-analysis of the GJ 229B dataset, the most complete available spectra for a T-dwarf, aiming to resolve the long-standing discrepancies in atmospheric models. While previous studies yielded inconsistent results due to challenges in modeling complex chemistry and molecular opacity, APOLLO successfully resolved these issues by integrating a robust non-LTE chemistry solver and a vast spectral line database. Our analysis produced consistent solutions across multiple observables, indicating that the model accurately represents the dwarf's atmosphere. NewView introduces a dual representation learning architecture designed to predict videos from new camera perspectives. Although the well-mixed (BM) model often fails to capture the spatial intricacies of pathogen transmission, recent research indicates that the basic reproduction number ($R_0$)$ of the BM model can effectively forecast the probability of transmission in settings like hospital wards. However, the transmission dynamics of influenza in a city bus cannot, in our view, be adequately represented by the assumptions inherent in the well-mixed framework. The quantum diffraction and birefringence of light arising from the zero-point electromagnetic field at the interface of a dielectric represent highly subtle phenomena, necessitating rigorous theoretical modeling and precise experimental techniques for their observation. Stealing of information-bearing signals represents a significant threat to physical layer security, prompting the need for authentication mechanisms at this level. Building on prior research, this paper investigates authentication through observation of a signal at an Authenticated Key Generation (AKG) channel under conditions of additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). In this framework, both the legitimate parties and an adversary generate a shared secret key based on signal samples collected from the channel; however, all subsequent verifications must be conducted keylessly to ensure security. The proposed scheme encodes verification bits into time shifts applied to a specific waveform, utilizing the noise floor of AWGN channels to convey data without an encryption key. Mathematical analysis and simulation outcomes confirm that the proposed keyless authentication method is viable, even in the presence of an adversary attempting to inflict verification failures.

Twisted transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers have emerged as a prominent area of research due to the appearance of flat bands within specific moiré superlattices, which offer a unique platform for investigating strongly correlated electron systems. This study examines the properties of flat-band plasmons in these systems, demonstrating that they manifest as a new form of quasi-particle. We identify that these plasmons originate from charge density fluctuations around flat bands and are characterized by an extreme low effective plasma frequency alongside high damping. Furthermore, these features enable the visual recognition of flat-band plasmons via Raman spectroscopy, offering a fresh experimental method to detect the existence of flat bands in such materials.

Almost conformal Ricci soliton constitutes a newly defined geometric structure with significant potential for future study, achieved by merging almost Einstein manifolds with almost cosilian ones within the context of almost cosilian geometry. Stars and planets both drive mass outflows, yet the underlying mechanisms differ significantly. For stars, where surface gravity is weak, magnetic fields are the primary engine for wind acceleration, operating through the dissipation of Alfv\'en wave turbulence and the reconnection of field lines. In contrast, massive planets rely on gravity-driven escape mechanisms, often initiated by ionization processes such as photoionization or cosmic ray ionization. Although the physics governing stellar winds and magnetic activity has been extensively studied, analogous research on planetary ionization, mass loss, and magnetospheres remains in its early stages. This review examines the distinct drivers of mass loss for these celestial bodies, exploring how magnetic fields function in both regimes and highlighting the critical role of the surrounding plasma environment in regulating wind behavior.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect (SOPE) enables the modification of a material's intrinsic spin-orbit coupling (SOC) through interaction with an adjacent layer exhibiting strong SOC. In this study, we focus on the magneto-spectroscopic characterization of Bi/Co multilayers to investigate the SOPE within the Bi substrate. Our analysis reveals that the Bi/Co interface is rough, resulting in intermixing and the formation of a cobalt-rich interfacial region. Consequently, the observed changes in spin-orbit splitting are driven primarily by the emergence of an interfacial magnetic phase rather than a pure pure Bi/Co effect alone. Furthermore, spectral analysis indicates that spin-orbit coupling is spatially inhomogeneous across the structure. Finally, we examine the correlation between the spin-orbit splitting energy and the thickness of the magnetic layer to extract quantitative parameters regarding the induced SOC.

This study derives exact bound state solutions for the time-independent, N-dimensional fractional Schrödinger equation utilizing the generalized Mie-type potential. By applying the factorization method within the framework of the fractional differential operator defined by Jumarie, we determine both the generalized fractional spectrum and the corresponding wave functions through explicit formulas. Additionally, expressions for the energy eigenvalues and factors are provided as functions of the potential's parameters. The validity and accuracy of these results are substantiated through comparison with existing literature. This study explores imposing explicit Lipschitz constraints on neural network architectures to ensure stability with respect to inputs. We introduce a method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for typical feedforward layers and use it to frame neural network training as a constrained optimization task. By employing proximal gradient descent, we enforce these bounds to produce training models with guaranteed bounds on their global Lipschitz constants. We further develop a general framework for the retuning of pre-trained networks under imposed Lipschitz limits. Our experimental results indicate that this regularization method enhances model accuracy and delivers significant reductions in inference costs by enabling larger input jumps during inference.

Neural sequence-to-sequence models have largely replaced rule-based methods for machine translation, largely due to their high empirical success. Yet, despite this performance, there remains a lack of understanding regarding the sequences' internal mechanics. This paper investigates whether these sequences can master textural concordances in Basque—a language renowned for its intricate morphological agreement systems. Through experiments utilizing both a high-concord and a low-concord variant of Basque, we observe that sequence models trained on the high-concord version generate outputs that maintain strict concord levels, whereas those trained on the low-concord variant produce language with diminished agreement. Crucially, the model demonstrates the capacity to learn these global summary statistics; we further validate this adaptability by demonstrating successful transfer learning when applying the high-concord translator to generate the low-concord variant.

The upcoming James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) will enable numerous observations of highly eccentric exoplanets, facilitating significant advancements in our understanding of planetary dynamics. To maximize the utility of JWST, optimizing the scheduling of observations across multi-telescope setups is essential. To this end, we employed data from a global network of observatories, utilizing the unique visibility windows provided during planetary transits to refine the ephemeris of planet HD 8066 b. Our analysis reveals a notable discrepancy between our updated orbital period and a previously published value; the old data relied on a limited dataset and failed to account for the non-linear timing variations associated with eccentric planetary motion. Consequently, our newly published ephemeris incorporates recent transit observations and accounts for these relativistic effects, ensuring precise prediction of future transit windows for effective integration with global telescope scheduling.

This study examines how models of foundation gameplay can inform the creation of therapeutic exercises for physical rehabilitation, specifically addressing shoulder range-of-motion limitations. We present an exersing game designed to support this recovery process and explore its potential for developing future medical games. The analysis applies Erwin's (2019) framework, which categorizes foundational gameplay elements into four categories: physical, mental, social, and fictional interactions. Furthermore, the article introduces a design methodology for creating exercise games grounded in foundation gameplay models and demonstrates its application through the development of our prototype.

The user proposed an indirect variational framework to analyze Iwaniec's problem regarding gradient Young measure selection, initially introduced in *arXiv:2105.00161*. This problem involves choosing a single element from a gradient Young measure $\nu$ on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, specifically minimizing an integral of the von Mises equivalent stress. The initial work established the problem's viability by defining a total energy functional composed of local stress terms integrated over $\Omega$ alongside a term representing surface defects in the chosen function. While the local stress satisfies convexity, it fails to be locally integrable, complicating standard direct methods.

To address this, the current work reformulates the setting within a $\Gamma$-convergence approach using phase-field approximation. This approximation replaces the piecewise-rigid structure of the original functional with one applicable to piecewise-$\mathrm{H}^1$-rigid functions. Within this new framework, it proves the existence of a global minimizer. Furthermore, it verifies that this minimizer belongs to the local stress-support of the initial Young measure $\nu$.

As an added advantage, this method provides a practical means to approximate piecewise-rigid functions using piecewise-rigid maps.

Reducing radiation exposure in positron emission tomography (PET) scans is a priority, yet it remains a significant challenge. Deep learning methods offer a potential solution for dose reduction, but they struggle with out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs and often produce over-smoothed results. To address these issues, we propose a new approach that reduces dose while maintaining accuracy and managing OOD data effectively. Our uncertainty-aware framework integrates physics-based constraints with a distribution-specific adapter network. This method employs an overall strategy to reduce the probability of OOD errors, complemented by a new module that mitigates OOD impacts by leveraging out-of-domain-free data to handle them. Furthermore, we introduce a boundary-aware module to ensure smooth transitions between OOD and in-domain regions. We validate our approach using the large-scale, multi-dose LUNA16 dataset, demonstrating superior performance across single- and multi-input doses compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques.

"From the moment we customize our smartphones, laptops, and cars to the way we curate our social media profiles, the practice of personalization serves as a defining feature of contemporary life. Yet, this same mechanism that fosters a sense of self can simultaneously obscure and reshape it. This paper explores the complex dynamics between customization, privacy, and the construction of identity. It examines how our interactions with privacy-sensitive technologies challenge our understanding of 'I' and 'mine,' while also investigating how these concepts can be leveraged to advance more equitable forms of self-presentation."

Centering theory (CT), a linguistic theory addressing the local coherence of discourse through the concept of centering, has historically been applied to coreference resolution. This study introduces a novel probabilistic centering framework utilizing a recurrent neural architecture to represent the shift in discourse centers via a set of centering features. Empirical results demonstrate that this probabilistic approach significantly surpasses the performance of the established CT-based method. Furthermore, the study analyzes the contribution of each feature individually, offering valuable insights regarding the effectiveness of centering features in improving coreference resolution accuracy.

WiFi Ranging is a geolocation technology designed to determine the distance between a user and a smartphone equipped with a WiFi radio. This study presents a framework for WiFi range estimation that employs supervised machine learning. Initially, it utilizes data collected from a single access point to train the model. Subsequently, the approach is expanded to incorporate access point triangulation capabilities. Finally, the method is improved by integrating multiple access point data to enhance triangulation accuracy. Key features extracted from raw Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) values are used to form the basis of this feature selection process.

The concept of a black hole, first theorized in the early 20th century, has recently been supported by observations of stellar remnants and the Event Horizon Telescope's direct imaging. This study explores whether the gravitational pull acting on an infinite, uniform, spherical distribution of matter could cause it to collapse and form a rigid shell that hovers at a fixed distance from a black hole—essentially a version of the Dyson Shell concept utilizing gravity instead of propulsion. While prior investigations into similar shells orbiting ordinary stars yielded negative results, our analysis reveals that such shells could theoretically exist around black holes, settling at a specific stable radius determined solely by the black hole's mass and the material's compressive strength. This stable orbital distance ranges from approximately 14 to roughly 300 times the Schwarzschild radius. Although the formation mechanism involves dynamic instabilities, the resulting configuration offers a novel, untested model distinct from both the black hole analogues proposed by Dyson and the gravitational shell models suggested by Vachaspati.

This paper examines the challenge of validating Service Level Agreement (SLA) breaches in virtualized, decentralized environments. It highlights the limitations of existing solutions, which typically rely on a centralized component to collect data and identify violations—a dependency that creates performance bottlenecks and single points of failure. Consequently, this study advocates for a peer-to-persistent (P2P) based approach designed to decentralize both communication and decision-making processes specifically regarding breach detection. The proposed methodology outlines necessary data structures and logic to facilitate a lightweight overlay network optimized for efficient violation identification. Performance evaluations demonstrate that this P2P framework delivers comparable results to a centralized benchmark while offering distinct advantages in terms of scalability and robustness.

Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs) function by having high-current microbunches traverse the same radiation damage-prone components twice: initially as unbunched, high-energy particles and subsequently as slightly lower-energy particles that have been filled into a bunch structure. A primary objective of this research is to determine the transverse beam instability, specifically beam breakdown instability (BBI), for both passes in an ERL test facility located at the Advanced Photon Source. This facility incorporates a chopper and vacuum pump station situated between the linac exit and reentry radiation damage-prone components. To address the current study's primary goal, we examine the influence of re-filling filling pattern design on BBI. We conduct this analysis using a newly developed numerical algorithm that integrates particle tracking, macro-particle modeling, and impedance calculations to calculate BBI. The results indicate that filling pattern configuration plays a significant role in shaping the re-entrant BBI spectrum. Furthermore, increasing the number of particles per macro-particle in the model improves the accuracy of the calculated results.

Precise knowledge of neutron interaction cross-sections is fundamental to advancing nuclear physics and engineering disciplines such as energy generation, medical technology, and waste disposal. Neutron scattering experiments remain the primary method for determining these cross-sections; however, achieving high-precision energy resolution in the MeV range is challenging because it necessitates sophisticated detector setups and the generation of narrowly bunched neutron pulses. This study introduces a new approach utilizing a 3D-position readout scintillator to track neutron trajectories in a magnetic field, thereby identifying exactly which neutrons interacted within the target. By confining neutrons to circular orbits via the field and analyzing the post-interaction path radii, one can deduce their initial kinetic energies. Consequently, neutron energies can be resolved with remarkable accuracy—nearly 1% precision at 5 MeV—enabling future high-precision total cross-section measurements in neutron pulses as short as 100 ps.

Previous laboratory studies on dust aggregation at cryogenic temperatures indicate that ice coatings enhance sticking strength, potentially allowing planetesimals to form in the low-density midplanes of protoplanetary disks. This study investigates how water ice's influence on sticking properties evolves at higher temperatures. We conducted collision experiments at 150 K, 200 K, and 300 G, utilizing two distinct grain mixtures: bare silicates paired with either bare silicates or silicates bearing an icy mantle on the silicate core, where the ice was either pure H2O or a H2O/D2O mixture. Our findings reveal that the increase in adhesion strength provided by ice persists at 150 K and 200 K, but this enhancement disappears at 300 K, where ice no longer has a significant impact on adhesion. Furthermore, the sublimation temperature for the sticking properties mirrors that observed in vapor mass loss experiments, suggesting that the critical factor is the presence of surface ice rather than bulk ice. These findings have significant implications for dust evolution and planet formation models operating beyond the traditional ice line.

This research examines the recursive least squares (RLS) method used for detecting spatially varying signals, where parameters change slowly over time and are modeled as an autoregressive (AR) process. A suite of user-friendly web-based tools has been created to visualize imaging and spectral data, with the primary objective of offering an accessible, open-source, and cost-free alternative to commercial software.
