Sequential sampling methods determine each sample based on the previously drawn observations, utilizing this information to enhance the efficiency of statistical estimates. Although these techniques have been highly effective for decades, they inherently produce estimates with low variance that fail to reflect the full diversity of a population, leading to highly similar and spatially clustered results across different runs. To address this limitation in the context of crowdsourcing and online surveys, we introduce a novel class of sampling plans designed to balance statistical efficiency with spatial variability. Our approach adapts Classic Dijkstra's sampling to incorporate a set of orthogonal estimation targets, enabling adaptive control of variance and coefficient of variance specifically for each parameter. Evaluation through both real-world and simulated datasets confirms that our method successfully achieves equitable spatial coverage while maintaining rigorous statistical efficiency.

We introduce a learning-based technique to correct extrinsic parameters for eye-in-hand cameras using only a single image. Although the method was developed for a single degree of freedom (1-DoF) calibration, it can be extended to more complex systems, including those with multiple degrees of freedom. By leveraging recent advancements in neural networks, this approach requires only minimal manual intervention, such as identifying a feature in 3D space and its corresponding projection in the image plane. Specifically, the user marks a cylindrical axis in the scene and identifies its silhouette in the image. The neural component then estimates the current extrinsic parameters by aligning a rendered model of the cylinder axis with the observed feature in the scene. The three-dimensional position of the axis is known beforehand, and the user can easily locate it. The system described is flexible, allowing the addition of new axes or cylinders as long as their 3D coordinates are accessible. The neural aspect of the technique is inherently extensible for incorporating multiple feature sets. The primary advantage of this system is the ability to adjust extrinsic parameters dynamically and in real time, a significant challenge in the current state of robotics. The method was evaluated on an industrial robotic arm equipped with a KUKA YUKO camera, demonstrating measurement accuracy within approximately 1 millimeter.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (CGGANs) have demonstrated significant potential in image-to-image translation and image restoration tasks. In this work, we introduce Conditional GANs with Weighted W\*_2 regularization to address ill-posed inverse problems. We establish that if the conditional generator $G$ belongs to the Hölder space $C^{0,\alpha}$ with $\alpha \in (0,1]$, the regularizer remains well-defined provided the mapper $T$ is $\beta$-Hölder continuous for some $\beta \in (0,\min(2\alpha,1))$. Assuming $G$ is an affine operator, we derive convergence rate bounds for the regularized conditional GAN framework. Furthermore, we propose a novel affine generator tailored for GANs regularized with WS\*_2^\alpha$$. Experiments on deconvolution and convolution-blending datasets indicate that this proposed methodology outperforms existing approaches in terms of reconstruction error and visual fidelity.

This paper investigates the effect of fractional differentiation on the absence of invariant surfaces within dynam systems. It is well established that fractional systems offer an advantage over their integer-order counterparts by offering an equivalent number of degrees of freedom while occupying fewer dimensions; for instance, a fractional system requires only three parameters to match the dynamic behavior of a standard system with four. In this study, we determine the conditions leading to the emergence of invariant surfaces in fractional systems and demonstrate these findings through a specific example.

Terahertz (THz) communications are recognized as promising pathways for future 6G mobile networks, offering vast bandwidths that support extreme data transmission rates. However, deploying THz signals over multi-hop routes presents significant hurdles, primarily due to extensive hardware hardware requirements and difficulties in maintaining stable signal integrity. A critical obstacle in this domain is the necessity for rapid and efficient beam training to identify optimal communication links. This study proposes leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to enhance beam training protocols specifically for THz systems operating across multi-hop environments. In this framework, learning agents autonomously acquire the optimal sequence of beams by interacting with the surrounding state space. The research introduces two distinct RL methodologies: a basic approach that trains a single universal policy to determine beams for all hops independently, and an advanced multi-agent hierarchical structure designed to learn individualized beam configurations for each segment of the link. Comprehensive simulations demonstrate that these suggested methods surpass traditional benchmark techniques by substantially improving end-to-end throughput, total transmission rate, and overall system efficiency.

The radio emission from pulsar B1133+16 is being utilized to conduct a sensitive investigation into the interstellar medium (ISM) along the line of sight at a 1.4 GHz wavelength. The analysis examines both the longitudinal and transverse characteristics of the scattering medium. Scintillation indices ($m^2$) were calculated for three distinct frequencies (1366, 1405, and 1420 MHz) by performing an autocorrelation analysis on 14 days of continuous All-Sky Monitor (ASM) data from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory. These results were compared against predictions from a longitudinal model, which was refined using previous measurements of spectral distortion and transverse scattering distributions. A high-resolution (approximately 100 km) model, constructed via a Bayesian approach, identifies a prominent electron density clump with a density of $10^6 cm^{-3}$ and a size of roughly 100 km located at a distance of 2.4 kpc. This finding aligns closely with a separate dense cloud inferred from spectral modeling. Furthermore, a halo model was developed to explain the observed consistency in transverse scattering profiles across the frequency spectrum. While this halo is positioned at 2.3 kpc, it is distinct from the dense clump described above.

This study introduces Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an advanced automatic music generation model designed to overcome the limitations of WaveNet by utilizing a parameterized pitch-conditioned expanded convolution to replace the standard fully connected layers. Unlike previous fully conditional generative models in music, which require massive network capacities and vast training data to produce complex structures, QPNet achieves comparable or superior performance with significantly fewer parameters. Furthermore, the modular expansion of its convolutional architecture facilitates the integration of domain-specific knowledge, allowing for the incorporation of musical theory to guide generation. Experimental evaluations confirm that QPNet excels in generating high-fidelity, artifact-free audio, surpassing the capabilities of WaveNet and other state-of-the-art fully conditional generative models.

Arabic is a highly morphologically complex language characterized by non-concatenative morphology, numerous roots, and significant morphophonemic variations. These complexities, combined with widely used script features like tashkeel (vowel diacritics) and variations in orthography, create substantial challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. While numerous annotated datasets exist for other languages, the scarcity of high-quality morphological annotation datasets hinders the advancement of Arabic NLP. To address this gap, we introduce MADARi, the first web platform dedicated to providing joint morphological annotation and spelling correction for news articles. The platform offers essential tools for linguists and researchers, including an auto-annotation feature that supports efficient data creation. Furthermore, it provides a robust environment for conducting experiments and utilizing pre-processed datasets. Finally, we released a dataset comprising 20,000 sentences annotated with both morphological information and spelling corrections, along with a set of baseline models designed to establish a benchmark for future research.

We introduce a new computational framework designed to model the spectral signatures and photochemistry of temperate, low-gravity exoplanets exposed to ultraviolet radiation and external fluxes of minor species. Our approach integrates a photochemical network capable of handling complex UV-driven reactions and photodissociation events with a one-dimensional horizontal energy balance equation that accounts for the fluxes of inactive tracers. This equation is solved self-consistently to simulate the effects of UV irradiation and the addition of external species on a planet's temperature. We applied this framework to investigate the spectral characteristics of Venus-analogs, focusing specifically on the UV spectra observed by the upcoming EXoplanet UV Spectrograph (EXUS) on the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). Our results indicate that the instrument can detect the accretion of externally supplied species, such as sulfur dioxide ($SO_2$) and carbon monoxide ($CO$), in the atmosphere. Furthermore, the model predicts that a Venus-like world would exhibit a temperature inversion and unique spectral features in both the temperature profile and chemical distribution resulting from UV exposure and the addition of these species. While the model is currently limited to a single vertical level, it offers a vital foundation for future multi-level simulations of temperate, chemically dynamic low-gravity exoplanets.

We examine normal-metal–semiconductor tunneling spectroscopy to investigate Majorana bound states (MBS) within a single topological superconducting contact. In this setup, the intrinsic Majorana peak appears at zero bias ($V=0$), yet it can be obscured by broadening from inelastic scattering or conductance steps caused by parallel conduction channels. To address this, we propose calculating the differential conductance for tunneling current through resistive electrodes at dissipation levels ranging from weak to strong ohmic dissipation. Our analysis indicates that an Majorana peak remains distinguishable from other features even under highly dissipative conditions, whereas spurious peaks generated by the electrode resistance shift away from zero bias as dissipation increases. We validate these findings with a model based on resonant Andreev reflection (RAR) for Majorana peaks and a Fabry-Pérot interferometry framework (incorporating elastic and dissipative factors) for electrode-induced peaks. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of experimentally detecting MBS in topological chains using this tunneling method combined with ohmic dissipation.

The swift advancement of deep-learning-driven intelligent detection protocols has yielded significant breakthroughs in automated road anomaly identification and digitized asset administration. Nevertheless, creating a precise detection model for surface flaws like potholes and cracks demands vast collections of annotated data, a task that is notoriously labor-intensive and costly. Furthermore, the reliance on data annotation creates substantial bottlenecks, hindering the efficient expansion of data repositories. To overcome these obstacles, we present **RoadAtlas**, an end-to-end intelligent framework designed to streamline the automatic retrieval, pre-processing, and labeling of data streams from diverse sources, thereby expediting the augmentation of road anomaly datasets. Complementing this data solution, RoadAtlas offers a comprehensive management interface that facilitates the full lifecycle oversight of real-world road conditions. By integrating a state-of-the-label detection framework, the platform delivers an accessible interface for the continuous and reliable monitoring of pavement defects.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) function as a potent framework for handling graph-structured data, yet they typically disregard the intrinsic structural details of individual graphs. This shortcoming is particularly problematic for temporal graphs, where incorporating evolution is essential for high performance. To address these issues, we introduce Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (LoGNN), a novel method designed to analyze data on "Lorentzian graphs." These graphs consist of nodes with attributes and directed edges characterized by both specific types and temporal latency. We outline the theoretical underpinnings of our approach, demonstrating its capacity to effectively integrate multi-granularity neighborhood aggregation across various temporal scopes while preserving the precise layout of nodes. Rigorous experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques for link prediction in temporal graphs. Our codebase can be accessed at https://github.com/lo-gnn/LoGNN.

This work examines the generation of photon number states (Fock states) using long-lived mechanical oscillators coupled with photons via radiation pressure. The study focuses on a single-mode cavity where nonlinear interactions are mediated by a two-level system in a specific superposition of energy levels, enabling a hybrid system to achieve both state-dependent reflection and position-dependent transmission. These dual conditional nonlinearities facilitate optical compression transfer, which, combined with a Markovian environment and a red-detuned single photon, facilitates optomachanical squeezing of a longer-lived mechanical mode. The protocol is validated through a comparison of a three-level system implementation, demonstrating that a simple two-level setup with tailored superposition can produce a highly similar result.

This paper introduces a modification to vectorial $\mu$-calculus that incorporates universal quantification and existential skolemization within a new class of "entities." We establish a characterization of this formulaic scope using first-order $\mu$-calculus formulas. Additionally, we confirm that the proposed entity-based system retains the decision procedures and temporal logic expressiveness inherent in the original formulation. Finally, we define a translation for LTL into the entity-formulas of first-order $\mu$-calculus, thereby extending the known expressive hierarchy of temporal logic to encompass formulas featuring the devised decision procedure.

If a signed graph admits a double cover with a connected component, it possesses the property of expandedness, for which we determine general bounds on expansion. As additional applications, we establish new results regarding the chromatic and choromatic numbers of the M\"obius ladder and complete bipartite graphs.

Let $A$ be a finite subset of $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and let $\Sigma A$ represent the collection of all possible signed sums formed by elements of $A$. This paper investigates the growth rate of $|\Sigma A|$ under the condition that $A$ exhibits restricted growth, defined as $\left|\Sigma B\right| \le k \left|B\right|$ for every subset $B \subset A$. Under these conditions, we establish direct results demonstrating that $\left|\Sigma A\right|$ remains polynomially bounded. Conversely, our findings indicate that in certain scenarios, the most significant contribution to $\left|\Sigma A\right|$ originates from signed sums involving the largest elements of $A$.

Although surgical removal effectively prevents colorectal cancer, the condition remains a leading global cause of death due to low rates of early detection and diagnosis. During colonoscopy examinations, physicians identify and remove precancerous growths known as colorectal polyps; however, manually assessing the risk of these polyps to determine appropriate surveillance intervals is a labor-intensive and subjective process. Consequently, there is a critical need for robust computer-aided systems capable of assisting pathologists in detecting and classifying these lesions. This study introduces UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset comprising 1,557 images of colorectal polyps annotated with risk categories by expert pathologists. We implemented a multi-task deep learning framework designed to automatically classify colorectal polyps and identify adenoma abnormalities using semi-supervised data labeling strategies. Evaluated on this dataset, our method achieves accuracy rates of 96.1% for polyp classification and 98.5% for adenoma abnormality grading, respectively. Furthermore, our approach significantly outperforms strong baseline models in terms of data efficiency, effectively leveraging the provided labels across the dataset.

This study introduces a novel numerical framework designed to solve time-harmonic acoustic scattering problems across unbounded domains, specifically targeting smooth coefficient variations and high-frequency regimes. In this context, smoothly varying coefficients preclude the application of standard boundary integral equation methods, while the high-frequency regime necessitates a fine discretization, presenting a combined challenge for efficient solution strategies. The proposed approach achieves a balanced trade-off between computational efficiency and numerical precision. It integrates a modified Helmholtz Green's function with a finite element method utilizing a locally adaptive mesh refinement process. Adaptive refinement is triggered by the local oscillation of the coefficient matrix, while the adaptive step size for the discrete time-stepping scheme is governed by the local smoothness of that matrix. Consequently, the resulting time-domain scheme allows for coarse initial discretizations, with the spatial grid automatically enhancing itself over successive time steps to maintain accuracy. We establish the method's convergence properties and validate them through numerical experiments.

The formation timeline and growth history of early solar system planetesimals are primarily reconstructed through the thermal evolution recorded in meteorites. A pivotal mechanism in this process is the impact of inner system planetesimals, a scenario supported by the widespread presence of impact melt rocks in chondrites and the specific alteration of ordinary chondrites by the Chelyabinsk impact event approximately 1.1 million years ago. This study presents new cratering age determinations for Chelyabinsk at 1.097 ± 0.013 million years and Benenitra at 1.101 ± 0.013 million years, utilizing the U-Pb isotopic system in allanite and the 53Mn-53Cr isotopic system in pyroxene. The precise alignment of these ages with the Hf-W derived inner solar system accretion age of 1.1 million years (± 0.1 million years) indicates that planetesimal formation concluded by this time. Furthermore, the small size of the Chelyabinsk impactor, inferred to be 1.101 ± 0.013 million years, suggests it caused minimal heating to surrounding planetesimals. Consequently, the inner solar system's planetesimals likely reached their 1.101 ± 0.013 million years, ending the era of significant accretion during this period.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we examine form factors for certain integrable XXZ models with higher-spin interactions. Our analysis reveals that these form factors exhibit an $\mathcal{H}_\text{affine} $ $q$-Yanjan-Dexter $Y$-symmetry, where the quantum group $U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_+) $ plays a crucial role. Specifically, we establish a connection between this symmetry and the $R$-matrix of the associated Yanjan-Dexter $Y$-model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the matrix elements of the symmetry operator within the Bethe anserm basis follow a specific structural pattern.

Voice translation (VTC) converts spoken language from one tongue into another, playing a vital role in global communication. State-of-the-art neural models for VTC rely heavily on extensive parallel corpora covering all supported language pairs, a requirement that significantly hampers support for low-resource languages. To circumvent this limitation, we introduce Zero-shot Voice Translation (Z-VTC), enabling synthetic speech conversion for pairs lacking available audio-parallel data. Our method integrates two core elements: an unsupervised alignment module that extracts synchronized features from monolingual sources without needing annotation, followed by a neural architecture that synthesizes spoken audio using these extracted features to achieve VTC capability. We evaluated our system across eight languages using the LibriSpeech corpus, employing Wav2Vec 2.0 for speech extraction and evaluating results using the Mozilla Common Voice dataset. Our approach was tested on eight language pairs with abundant data for single-source languages but sparse or absent for parallel sets. Compared to a strong baseline, our system improves performance by 1.5 to 2.5 Mozilla TCTO (TCTO) scores, with the largest relative gains observed in low-resource scenarios. We have released our codebase publicly at https://github.com/your-org/Z-VTC.

The conventional electrostatic and near-field approximations, typically valid when the light wavelength far exceeds the target object's dimensions, employ a multipole expansion to describe light-matter interactions. While these methods are well-established for optical scattering and near-field radiation forces, they require modification for light propagation and material responses within the near-resonant regime (where the wavelength is comparable to the object size). This article details a general computational framework for multiple scatterers in this near-resonant regime, incorporating both light propagation and material response. Specifically, we address the limitations of standard multipole basis sets by adapting them for near-resonant conditions. We apply these techniques to analyze forces acting on nanoparticles, focusing on near-resonant trapping radiation forces and newly identified non-resonant forces generated by the interference of multipoles within the focal volume.

We examine the scoto-seesaw framework within an $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ supersymmetric extension, incorporating the required Higgs triplets to generate a Type-II neutrino seesaw mechanism. Our analysis investigates the stability of the electroweak vacuum and the stability matrix in detail. We establish constraints on the model's parameter space by incorporating experimental data from LEP, the Tevatron, LHC, and neutrino oscillillation observations, alongside recent findings regarding the Higgs boson mass. Furthermore, we propose a WIMP dark matter scenario utilizing the inert neutral component of the triplet fermion as the dark matter candidate. Finally, we delineate the regions compatible with both the correct dark matter relic density and a stable electroweak vacuum within the broader context of this unified theory.

We introduce the concept of relative quantum geometry of complex manifolds with respect to a morphism. For a smooth compact complex variety $X$ and a morphism $f: X \to Y$ where $Y$ is irreducible, we demonstrate that relative quantum homology and relative Gromov-Witten invariants can be defined. These invariants are shown to possess the standard deformation invariance property with respect to variations of relative algebraic complex structures on families $(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y}, \mathcal{F}) \subset \mathcal{A}$ such that the map is flat and the generic fiber defines a deformation of relative complex structure. Furthermore, we establish the correspondence between relative quantum homology and relative stable maps utilizing multisections of morphisms $\mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ within such families. Our primary application involves proving the preservation of relative quantum homology under morphisms of varieties admitting a relative Mori fiber type. As a direct outcome, we derive formulas expressing the quantum pullback map in terms of the ordinary geometric pullback map.

Although Image Augmentation (IA) is a fundamental step in creating deep learning models for medical image analysis, existing methods often neglect the semantic content of the images, resulting in unrealistic alterations that may not reflect physiological plausibility. Although some recent Illness-aware Image Augmentation (IIA) approaches have been proposed to address this, they remain untested on the specific nuances of chest X-rays (CXR). To date, no available solution exists for modifying the anatomy within a CXRX while preserving clinical relevance. To bridge this gap, we introduce the first set of CXRX-specific augmentation methods designed to modify patient symptoms and visual appearances. Using the CheXpert dataset, we evaluate these new techniques against traditional ones. The results indicate that our proposed approach generates more diverse and realistic variations of the data, leading to a 10% improvement in performance for a DenseNet-121 classifier trained on CXRX retake tasks.

Nonlinear visualization and analysis of geographical vector datasets are crucial for various expert domains, including meteorology, oceanography, and geology. These fields depend on visual representations to comprehend atmospheric and environmental dynamics, a necessity driven by the fact that physical phenomena rarely map linearly onto 2D spatial coordinates. While existing software for meteorological visualization offers advanced rendering features, they often lack user-friendliness and fail to provide interactive statistical analysis. To bridge this gap, we present ViDaExpert, a desktop application designed for the intuitive visualization and analysis of multidimensional vectorial data. Written in Python with a Qt interface, the tool supports data formats such as GRIB and CSV. It enables the rendering of points, lines, and contours across various viewing modes, including orthographic, geographic, and stereoscopic projections. Additionally, users can perform statistical analyses through scatter plots and diagrams, extract data points along specific trajectories, and generate professional reports. Equipped with robust path import and export functions, as well as full 3D modeling capabilities, ViDaExpert offers comprehensive analysis and flexible visual output for multidimensional vectorial datasets.

Employing an approach inspired by the work of Scully et al. (SIAM J. Sci. Furthermore, this method is generalized to handle singularities arising from densities with weaker moments, as well as those defined on domains composed of irregular shapes. Practical experiments confirm that this algorithm maintains a computational complexity of $O(N \log N)$, where $N$ denotes the count of density's underlying support elements.

In this study, we present the practical implementation of a computational framework designed to efficiently evaluate the Newtonian potential for densities confined to planar regions. By integrating techniques typically associated with fast multipole algorithms (FMM) and local singular expansions, our approach achieves rigorous efficiency when utilizing standard computational schemes. Furthermore, this method has been expanded to effectively manage singularities related to densities exhibiting moment deficiencies, as well as defined on domains characterized by irregular geometries. Empirical evidence confirms that this algorithm operates with a computational complexity of $O(N \log N)$, where $N$ is the count of elements comprising the density's underlying support, thereby ensuring both accuracy and high performance.
